What Time Is It? How Data Geometry Makes Time Conditioning Optional for Flow Matching

Alec Helbling ††thanks: Corresponding author: alechelbling@gatech.edu Affiliation: Georgia Tech    Sebastian Gutierrez Hernandez Affiliation: Georgia Tech    Benjamin Hoover Affiliation: Georgia Tech & IBM Research    Duen Horng Chau Affiliation: Georgia Tech    Parikshit Ram Affiliation: IBM Research
Abstract

Recent work has shown that models flow matching models can be trained without explicit time conditioning, challenging the standard view that the interpolation time is needed to disambiguate velocity targets. But why should a time-blind model work at all? Decomposing the time-blind flow matching loss, we identify two sources of irreducible error: a coupling variance, which arises from ambiguous velocity targets induced by how noise and data points are paired, and the time-blindness gap, which is the additional error caused by ignoring time. This gap shows that time-blind training is strictly harder than conventional training, reinforcing the puzzle that time-blind models work so well in practice. We resolve this tension by showing that the geometry of high-dimensional data makes time identifiable directly from noisy observations. When data concentrates near a kk-dimensional subspace, time can be recovered from the statistical structure of noisy interpolants in directions orthogonal to the data; under a spiked-covariance model, this yields a closed-form estimator that recovers tt from a single observation zz at rate O⁡(1/d−k)O(1/\sqrt{d-k}) for ambient dimension dd. As a consequence, we prove that the time-blindness gap is asymptotically negligible relative to the coupling variance. We empirically demonstrate our identifiability result on real-world data and show that changing the coupling has a much larger effect on loss and sample quality than removing time conditioning across CIFAR-10, CelebA-HQ, and FFHQ. These results explain why time-blind flow matching works and show that the main practical lever is the choice of coupling, not explicit time conditioning.

1 Introduction

Flow matching [17, 1] has emerged as a leading framework for training generative models, learning a time-conditioned velocity field vθ​(z,t)v_{\theta}(z,t) that transports noise to data along interpolated paths. The time variable is usually treated as essential, under the intuition that conditioning on tt seems necessary to disambiguate between velocity targets when at the same spatial location. From this perspective, a time-blind vector field fθ​(z)f_{\theta}(z) should be fundamentally disadvantaged, since it must assign a single velocity to locations that may be reached by many trajectories at different times (Figure 2).

Recent work challenges this view. The performance of time-unconditional generative models often barely degrades at all when explicit conditioning is removed and sometimes even improves  [28, 31], and blind denoising analyses show that the noise level can sometimes be inferred from the noisy observation itself under low-dimensional data structure [13]. But for flow matching, this is not the whole story. Flow matching has another source of irreducible ambiguity: the coupling between noise and data during training. Even if time is known, many coupled pairs can pass through the same interpolant and induce different velocities. Thus the central question is not if a time-blind model can infer tt, but rather if the residual cost of hiding tt is large compared to the coupling-induced error that all flow matching models already pay.

The time-blind flow matching loss decomposes into a learnable approximation term, a coupling variance that remains even for an optimal time-conditioned predictor, and a time-blindness gap caused by averaging over unobserved times. The gap measures exactly how much harder time-blind training is than standard flow matching, and we show that in practical settings it is small. When data concentrates in a low-dimensional subspace, the interpolant’s component orthogonal to that subspace is supplied almost entirely by the Gaussian source, and its magnitude changes predictably with tt, a built-in statistical clock for the hidden time. We formalize this with an explicit estimator whose error shrinks with the residual ambient dimension, making the cost of hiding time negligible compared with the coupling variance. Coupling, not time conditioning, is the dominant lever.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    An explanatory loss decomposition for time-blind flow matching. We decompose the time-blind flow matching (FM) loss into a learnable error, an irreducible coupling variance shared with standard FM, and an additional time-blindness gap unique to time-blind flows (Proposition  1).

  2. 2.

    A constructive time-identification statistic for noisy interpolants. Under a spiked-covariance data model, the residual-subspace energy of a single interpolant zz yields a closed-form estimator of tt with error Op​(1/d−k)O_{p}(1/\sqrt{d-k}) (Theorem 2).

  3. 3.

    A relative bound showing that coupling dominates the cost of hiding time. Combining the decomposition with the identifiability rate, we prove that the time-blindness gap is smaller than the coupling variance by a factor O⁡(1/(d−k))O(1/(d-k)) (Theorem 3).

  4. 4.

    Empirical validation on real data and trained flow models. On CIFAR-10, CelebA-HQ, and FFHQ, the residual-subspace statistic recovers interpolation time at the predicted rate (Section 5.2), and trained models show that coupling has a much larger effect on loss and sample quality than explicit time conditioning (Section 5.1)

2 Problem Setup

In this section we present the theoretical formulation for understanding the core problems faced by conventional flow matching models, and more specifically by time-blind models that drop the time conditioning.

Flow matching.

Flow matching (FM) [17, 1] learns a time-conditioned velocity field vθ​(x,t)v_{\theta}(x,t) transporting a noise distribution p0p_{0} to a data distribution p1p_{1} over t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]. Given a coupling (ε,x)∼π(\varepsilon,x)\sim\pi with ε∼p0\varepsilon\sim p_{0} and x∼p1x\sim p_{1}, the linear interpolant defines a conditional path

z=(1−t)​ε+t​xz=(1-t)\,\varepsilon+t\,x (1)

with constant conditional velocity u=x−εu=x-\varepsilon. The model is trained to regress vθ​(z,t)v_{\theta}(z,t) onto uu:

ℒFM=𝔼t,(ε,x)∼π​[‖vθ​(z,t)−u‖2].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,\,(\varepsilon,x)\sim\pi}\left[\left\|v_{\theta}(z,t)-u\right\|^{2}\right]. (2)
Time-blind flow matching.

We consider a time-blind vector field fθ​(z)f_{\theta}(z) trained against the same interpolant-based regression target u=x−εu=x-\varepsilon. Given (ε,x)∼π(\varepsilon,x)\sim\pi and the interpolant z=(1−t)​ε+t​xz=(1-t)\varepsilon+tx with t∼𝒰⁡[0,1]t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1], the time-blind loss is

ℒTB=𝔼t,(ε,x)∼π​[‖fθ​(z)−u‖2].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TB}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,\,(\varepsilon,x)\sim\pi}\left[\left\|f_{\theta}(z)-u\right\|^{2}\right]. (3)

The key question is: what is the cost of dropping the time conditioning that FM relies on?

3 An Explanatory Decomposition of the Time-Blind Loss

The time-blind loss ℒTB\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TB}} mixes together errors of very different origins: some that any flow matching model must pay regardless of time conditioning, some that are unique to dropping tt, and some that the practitioner can drive away by training a better model. Pulling these apart is what lets us pose the central question of the paper precisely: how does the extra cost of hiding tt compare to the irreducible cost that flow matching pays anyway? Proposition 1 makes this separation exact.

3.1 The Three-Term Decomposition

We consider arbitrary time-blind vector fields f:ℝd→ℝdf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}. Throughout, unsubscripted 𝔼\mathbb{E} denotes expectation over the full joint (ε,x,t)∼π⊗𝒰⁡[0,1](\varepsilon,x,t)\sim\pi\otimes\mathcal{U}[0,1].

Proposition 1 (Anatomy of the Time-Blind Loss).

For any predictor f:ℝd→ℝdf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, the time-blind loss decomposes as

ℒTB​(f)=𝔼⁡[‖f⁡(z)−𝔼⁡[u∣z]‖2]⏟I. Learnable error+𝔼⁡[Var⁡(u∣z,t)]⏟II. Coupling variance ​𝒞π+𝔼[Var(𝔼[u∣z,t]|z)]⏟III. Time-Blindness Gap ​Δ.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TB}}(f)\;=\;\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|f(z)-\mathbb{E}[u\mid z]\|^{2}\bigr]}_{\text{I. Learnable error}}\;+\;\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{Var}(u\mid z,t)\bigr]}_{\text{II. Coupling variance }\mathcal{C}_{\pi}}\;+\;\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{Var}\bigl(\mathbb{E}[u\mid z,t]\,\big|\,z\bigr)\bigr]}_{\text{III. Time-Blindness Gap }\Delta}. (4)

(Proof in Appendix A.1.)

The decomposition is exact, holds for any ff, and requires no assumptions on the coupling or model class. Each term has a distinct origin and a distinct lever, which we now unpack in turn.

I. Learnable error.

This is the squared distance between the predictor and the optimal time-blind predictor f∗​(z):=𝔼⁡[u∣z]f^{*}(z):=\mathbb{E}[u\mid z]. It is the only term that depends on the choice of predictor, and the only one the practitioner can drive to zero: with sufficient capacity and data, fθ→f∗f_{\theta}\to f^{*} and this term vanishes.

II. Coupling variance.

This is the irreducible variance

𝒞π:=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(u∣z,t)]\mathcal{C}_{\pi}\;:=\;\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{Var}(u\mid z,t)\bigr]

of the regression target after conditioning on both zz and tt. This floor exists even if we grant the model the very information we are trying to hide: fixing (z,t)(z,t) does not fix the underlying pair (ε,x)(\varepsilon,x), since z=(1−t)​ε+t​xz=(1-t)\varepsilon+tx is one affine constraint on two variables. Distinct pairs that route through the same (z,t)(z,t) generally carry different velocities, and the best any predictor can do is predict their conditional mean v∗(z,t):=𝔼[u∣z,t]v^{*}(z,t):=\mathbb{E}[u\mid z,t], leaving residual variance 𝒞π\mathcal{C}_{\pi}. This floor is paid by the optimal time-conditioned predictor in standard flow matching too (Lemma A.1), and the time-blind model must at least inherit it. The size of 𝒞π\mathcal{C}_{\pi} is controlled entirely by the coupling π\pi: independent couplings permit many distinct (ε,x)(\varepsilon,x) to route through the same (z,t)(z,t) with disagreeing velocities, while structured couplings such as mini-batch optimal transport pair nearer points and tighten the conditional. This is the lever we manipulate in Section 4.2.

III. Time-blindness gap.

This is the additional price

Δ:=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(v∗​(z,t)∣z)]\Delta\;:=\;\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{Var}\bigl(v^{*}(z,t)\mid z\bigr)\bigr]

paid for not observing tt, on top of the coupling variance. A time-blind predictor cannot assign different velocities to the same location at different times (Figure 2), so at its optimum it must average v∗v^{*} over the posterior t|zt\mid z: f∗​(z)=𝔼⁡[v∗​(z,t)∣z]f^{*}(z)=\mathbb{E}[v^{*}(z,t)\mid z]. The gap Δ\Delta measures how much v∗v^{*} varies across this posterior — if zz nearly determines tt, the gap collapses. Since Δ≥0\Delta\geq 0 always (Corollary A.2), this term is unique to time-blind models and makes the time-blind optimum at least as hard as conventional flow matching.

4 Data Geometry Mitigates the Time-Blindness Gap

Proposition 1 reduces the puzzle to a comparison between two irreducible terms: the time-blindness gap Δ\Delta and the coupling variance 𝒞π\mathcal{C}_{\pi}. This section shows that, in high-dimensional low-rank regimes, the hidden time is already encoded in the geometry of the interpolant. In particular, the residual subspace provides a high-dimensional clock that identifies tt from zz alone. Once tt is nearly determined by zz, explicitly conditioning on tt adds little information, so the time-blindness gap is small. Under the spiked covariance model, this intuition yields the asymptotic comparison Δ/𝒞π=O⁡(1/(d−k))\Delta/\mathcal{C}_{\pi}=O(1/(d-k)), leaving the coupling variance as the dominant loss floor.

4.1 The Noise Subspace is a High-Dimensional Clock

Suppose the data x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} concentrates near a kk-dimensional signal subspace with k≪dk\ll d. Let U⟂∈ℝd×(d−k)U_{\perp}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times(d-k)} be an orthonormal basis for the orthogonal complement of this subspace, and let P⟂=U⟂​U⟂⊤P_{\perp}=U_{\perp}U_{\perp}^{\top} be the projection preserved by that basis. The key observation is that P⟂​zP_{\perp}z removes most of the data signal while retaining the ambient Gaussian source noise. Thus the residual energy ‖P⟂​z‖2\|P_{\perp}z\|^{2} changes predictably with the interpolation time tt.

Spiked covariance model.

To make this mechanism explicit, we analyze a standard spiked covariance model [12, 6, 30]

x∼𝒩⁡(0,Ux​Λ​Ux⊤+σ2​Id),x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\,U_{x}\Lambda U_{x}^{\top}+\sigma^{2}I_{d}),

where Ux∈ℝd×kU_{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} spans the signal subspace, Λ\Lambda contains the excess variances in the signal directions, and σ2​Id\sigma^{2}I_{d} is an isotropic residual floor. This model idealizes the empirical observation that natural data often has most of its variance in a low-dimensional subspace while retaining small residual variance in the remaining directions (Figure 3).

The residual variance clock.

Under this model, projection onto the orthogonal complement of UxU_{x} eliminates the spike directions. In each residual coordinate, P⟂​zP_{\perp}z combines an ambient Gaussian-noise coordinate with variance 11, scaled by (1−t)(1-t), and a residual data coordinate with variance σ2\sigma^{2}, scaled by tt. Since these terms are independent and centered, their variances add:

Var⁡[(P⟂​z)j]=(1−t)2​Var⁡(εj)+t2​Var⁡(xj)=(1−t)2+t2​σ2.\operatorname{Var}\!\left[(P_{\perp}z)_{j}\right]=(1-t)^{2}\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_{j})+t^{2}\operatorname{Var}(x_{j})=(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}\sigma^{2}.

Therefore,

P⟂​z∼𝒩⁡(0,σ⟂2​(t)​Id−k),σ⟂2​(t):=(1−t)2+t2​σ2.P_{\perp}z\;\sim\;\mathcal{N}\!\bigl(0,\;\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t)\,I_{d-k}\bigr),\qquad\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t)\;:=\;(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}\sigma^{2}. (5)

We call σ⟂2​(t)\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t) the variance clock. A high-dimensional isotropic Gaussian places almost all its mass on a thin shell of squared radius (d−k)​σ⟂2​(t)(d-k)\,\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t), with relative fluctuations of order 1/d−k1/\sqrt{d-k}, so observing the empirical radius of P⟂​zP_{\perp}z pinpoints the variance and hence tt. This gives a closed-form estimator on any branch where the clock is invertible:

σ^⟂2:=1d−k​‖P⟂​z‖2,t^​(z):=(σ⟂2)−1​(σ^⟂2).\widehat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}\;:=\;\frac{1}{d-k}\,\|P_{\perp}z\|^{2},\qquad\hat{t}(z)\;:=\;(\sigma_{\perp}^{2})^{-1}\!\bigl(\widehat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}\bigr). (6)

Because the shell concentrates at rate 1/d−k1/\sqrt{d-k}, this single-sample estimator recovers tt with vanishing error as the residual dimension grows, as shown in Theorem 2.

Theorem 2 (Identifiability of tt from zz; informal).

Under the spiked covariance model, on any interval where the noise-subspace variance clock identifies time, the estimator t^​(z)\hat{t}(z) in (6) satisfies

t^​(z)=t+Op​(1d−k).\hat{t}(z)\;=\;t\;+\;O_{p}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d-k}}\right).

(Formal statement and proof in Appendix B.2.)

Thus, removing explicit time conditioning does not necessarily remove time information. In high-dimensional low-rank regimes, the interpolant zz itself contains an implicit clock, so a sufficiently expressive time-blind predictor can infer the relevant time from geometry rather than from an external conditioning variable. The only caveat is that this clock is branchwise: σ⟂2​(t)\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t) decreases until its critical point t∗=1/(1+σ2)t^{*}=1/(1+\sigma^{2}) and increases thereafter, so the variance alone identifies tt only on intervals where this map is one-to-one. In our datasets, t∗t^{*} lies near the data endpoint, so the descending branch covers nearly the full interpolation path (Table C.3).

Beyond isotropic spectra.

The residual-clock mechanism does not rely on an exactly isotropic residual spectrum. For anisotropic Gaussian residuals, concentration is governed by the effective rank

reff​(ΣP,t):=(tr⁡ΣP,t)2tr⁡(ΣP,t2),ΣP,t:=(1−t)2​I+t2​ΣP,r_{\mathrm{eff}}(\Sigma_{P,t})\;:=\;\frac{(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{P,t})^{2}}{\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{P,t}^{2})},\qquad\Sigma_{P,t}\;:=\;(1-t)^{2}I+t^{2}\Sigma_{P},

which measures the number of projected directions that contribute appreciable variance. Thus the role played by d−kd-k in the spiked model is played more generally by reff​(ΣP,t)r_{\mathrm{eff}}(\Sigma_{P,t}) (Proposition B.1, Appendix B.4). We focus on the spiked model in the main text because it yields a closed-form inverse clock and a transparent comparison between the time-blindness gap and coupling variance (Theorem 3). Empirically, PCA-fitted residual spectra on real data have sufficiently large effective rank for the same prediction to track the observed estimator-error distributions (Section 5.2).

4.2 The Time-Blindness Gap is Negligible Relative to Coupling Variance

Theorem 2 shows that tt can be recovered from zz alone at rate Op​(1/d−k)O_{p}(1/\sqrt{d-k}). This directly controls the time-blindness gap in Proposition 1. Indeed, if tt is nearly determined by zz, then the time-aware optimal predictor v∗(z,t)=𝔼[u∣z,t]v^{*}(z,t)=\mathbb{E}[u\mid z,t] varies little over the posterior uncertainty t|zt\mid z. Equivalently, explicitly revealing tt adds little information beyond what is already present in zz. Under the spiked covariance model, this intuition yields a quantitative comparison between the extra cost of hiding time and the coupling variance already paid by time-conditioned flow matching.

Theorem 3 (Cost of Time-Independence; informal).

Under the spiked covariance model with independent coupling, on any interval where the noise-subspace variance clock identifies time, the time-blindness gap Δ\Delta and coupling variance 𝒞π\mathcal{C}_{\pi} satisfy

Δ𝒞π=𝔼[Var(𝔼[u∣z,t]∣z)]𝔼⁡[Var⁡(u∣z,t)]=O⁡(1d−k).\frac{\Delta}{\mathcal{C}_{\pi}}\;=\;\frac{\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{Var}\bigl(\mathbb{E}[u\mid z,t]\mid z\bigr)\bigr]}{\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{Var}(u\mid z,t)\bigr]}\;=\;O\!\left(\frac{1}{d-k}\right).

(Formal statement and proof in Appendix B.7.)

The rate is set by the noise-subspace dimension alone: holding kk fixed and growing dd gives the O⁡(1/d)O(1/d) scaling, while holding d−kd-k fixed and growing kk leaves the ratio bounded by a constant. This separates our account from purely ambient-dimension explanations of time identifiability [28], and we validate both regimes empirically in Sections 5.3 and 5.1.

Coupling as the dominant lever.

The coupling variance 𝒞π\mathcal{C}_{\pi} is not specific to time-blind models: by Lemma A.1, it is the irreducible floor paid even by the optimal time-conditioned predictor v∗(z,t)=𝔼[u∣z,t]v^{*}(z,t)=\mathbb{E}[u\mid z,t]. Theorem 3 shows that the additional price of removing time conditioning is lower order in the high-dimensional low-rank regime. Thus, once time is identifiable from zz, reducing 𝒞π\mathcal{C}_{\pi} should matter more than restoring explicit time conditioning. In our experiments, we reduce 𝒞π\mathcal{C}_{\pi} using mini-batch optimal transport [29, 9], which approximates the population OT map [3] by solving a linear assignment within each training batch.

5 Experiments

Our experiments confirm three core predictions of our theory. Section 5.1 confirms that the three-term decomposition is additive across paired (time conditioning, coupling) settings, with the coupling variance dominating the loss and mini-batch OT translating that dominance into sample-quality gains. Section 5.2 confirms that the noise-subspace estimator t^​(z)\hat{t}(z) matches its predicted error distribution on synthetic and real data. Section 5.2 shows that on the spiked Gaussian, the time-blindness gap is governed by the noise-subspace dimension d−kd-k rather than dd alone, and is dwarfed by the coupling variance across the (d,k)(d,k) plane.

We evaluate on two complementary settings: (1) Real image datasets. CIFAR-10 [16] in pixel space (d=3,072d{=}3{,}072) with an ADM UNet, and CelebA-HQ [14] and FFHQ [15] in Stable Diffusion VAE [25] latent space (d=4,096d{=}4{,}096) with a SiT-B/2 backbone [20], spanning two modalities and two architectures so that observed effects are not artifacts of either. (2) Synthetic spiked covariance. The Gaussian model of Section 4.1 with Λ\Lambda eigenvalues spaced linearly in [1,10][1,10] and σ2=0.1\sigma^{2}=0.1, where varying dd and kk directly sweeps the noise-subspace dimension d−kd-k that governs the rate in Theorem 2. (Details in Appendix C.1.)

5.1 The Decomposition is Additive and Coupling is the Dominant Lever

We train flow matching models on each dataset, varying (i) whether the model conditions on time tt or receives t=0t=0 at every step, and (ii) whether the coupling is independent or mini-batch OT (exact EMD solver). Each model is evaluated under its own training coupling, so the measured loss reflects the irreducible floor of the coupling it was trained with (details in Appendix C.2). Figure 4 and Table C.2 confirm three predictions:

  1. 1.

    Coupling and time conditioning appear to be distinct, approximately additive levers. If coupling and time conditioning act independently, switching from independent to OT coupling should produce a similar improvement with and without time conditioning. Across all three datasets, switching from independent to OT coupling produces nearly the same improvement in both the time-conditioned and time-blind rows. This suggests that improved coupling does not simply compensate for missing time information, and that removing time conditioning does not erase the benefit of OT coupling.

  2. 2.

    Coupling variance dominates the loss floor. The time-blindness gap should be small relative to the coupling effect on real, high-dimensional data (Section 4.2). On CIFAR-10 the coupling effect is roughly 25×25\times the time effect (dropping time conditioning costs <0.7%<\!0.7\% of total loss); on CelebA-HQ and FFHQ the time-blindness gap accounts for <2%<\!2\% of total loss.

  3. 3.

    OT coupling improves both loss and sample quality. Converged FID-50k mirrors the loss decomposition: OT coupling improves FID on every dataset regardless of whether the model is time-conditioned or time-blind, while the difference between time-conditioned and time-blind variants remains small (Table C.2, Appendix C.2).

5.2 Validating Time Identifiability on Real Data

Theorem 2 predicts that the interpolation time tt is recoverable from zz alone at rate O⁡(1/d−k)O(1/\sqrt{d-k}), with errors approximately Gaussian. We construct the noise-subspace estimator t^​(z)\hat{t}(z) from the proof and compare its empirical error distribution against the theoretical Gaussian on the synthetic spiked covariance model and on each of our three real datasets, fitting the spiked covariance via PCA at the 95%95\% explained-variance threshold for the theoretical prediction.

Fitting the spiked covariance to real data.

Given a dataset we compute the sample covariance Σ^\hat{\Sigma} and eigendecompose it as Σ^=V​diag​(λ^1,…,λ^d)​V⊤\hat{\Sigma}=V\,\mathrm{diag}(\hat{\lambda}_{1},\dots,\hat{\lambda}_{d})\,V^{\top} with eigenvalues sorted descending. At a chosen rank kk we set the signal subspace UxU_{x} to the top-kk eigenvectors, the isotropic floor σ2=1d−k​∑j>kλ^j\sigma^{2}=\frac{1}{d-k}\sum_{j>k}\hat{\lambda}_{j} to the mean of the trailing eigenvalues, and the spike eigenvalues Λi=max⁡(λ^i−σ2, 0)\Lambda_{i}=\max(\hat{\lambda}_{i}-\sigma^{2},\,0) for i≤ki\leq k, so that Ux​Λ​Ux⊤+σ2​IdU_{x}\Lambda U_{x}^{\top}+\sigma^{2}I_{d} recovers the empirical top-kk spectrum and collapses the residual tail into a single isotropic term. These parameters enter only the theoretical Gaussian prediction; the data xx in z=(1−t)​ε+t​xz=(1-t)\varepsilon+tx are actual samples drawn from the dataset, not from this Gaussian.

The theorem makes four confirmed predictions (details in Appendix C.3):

  1. 1.

    Predictions are tight in absolute terms. With d−kd-k in the thousands, the empirical estimates track closely around the true time on every panel. The empirical histograms are sharply peaked at zero and the spread shrinks as d−kd-k grows, consistent with the O⁡(1/d−k)O(1/\sqrt{d-k}) rate predicted by Theorem 2.

  2. 2.

    The closed-form estimator achieves the predicted rate on both synthetic and real data. Under the spiked Gaussian where Theorem 2’s assumptions hold exactly, the empirical histogram of t^−t\hat{t}-t tracks the theoretical Gaussian closely. The same prediction transfers to real, non-Gaussian data: fitting the spiked model via PCA yields a theoretical Gaussian that matches the empirical error distribution on CIFAR-10, FFHQ, and CelebA-HQ. The bound requires only that d−kd-k be large, not strict low-rank concentration, so even on VAE latents whose spectra are visibly flatter than pixel CIFAR-10 (Figure 3), d−kd-k remains in the thousands and the estimator achieves the predicted rate.

  3. 3.

    Approximate invertibility is not a major concern in practice. Because t∗t^{*} sits close to 11 on every dataset, the descending-branch inverse covers nearly the full interpolation path; even when tt is sampled uniformly over [0,1][0,1], the mean absolute error remains small on every dataset (0.0060.006 on CIFAR-10, 0.0210.021 on FFHQ, 0.0180.018 on CelebA-HQ; Appendix C.4).

5.3 Closed-Form Validation of the Variance Decomposition

To isolate the dimensional scaling predicted by our theory from confounds of training and finite-sample noise, we evaluate the three loss terms in an idealized spiked-covariance setting where each admits a closed-form or low-variance numerical estimator. Our analysis makes three sharp predictions about how the ambient dimension dd and signal dimension kk shape the three terms of Proposition 1. We test all three on the spiked Gaussian (details in Appendix C.5). Figure 6 reports each along a complementary slice of the (d,k)(d,k) grid.

  1. 1.

    Shrinking the noise subspace inflates the gap. At fixed dd, growing kk shrinks the (d−k)(d-k)-dimensional noise subspace through which tt leaks into zz, so the time-blindness gap should explode. At d=1024d=1024, sweeping kk blows up the gap (Figure 6, left).

  2. 2.

    Enlarging the ambient space collapses the gap. At fixed kk, growing dd enlarges the noise subspace and Theorem 3 predicts the ratio Δ/𝒞π\Delta/\mathcal{C}_{\pi} scales as 1/(d−k)1/(d-k). At k=64k=64, sweeping dd drives the gap toward zero while Terms I and III stay bounded (Figure 6, right).

  3. 3.

    Coupling variance dominates the gap across the plane. On the bulk of the (d,k)(d,k) plane (anywhere off the k≈dk\approx d diagonal), the coupling variance should dwarf the gap. The heatmap (center) is light everywhere except along the diagonal, and in both slice plots the coupling curve sits well above the gap throughout.

6 Related Work

Noise-level estimation and blind denoising.

Recovering the noise level from a corrupted observation is a classical problem in image processing, with estimators based on local image statistics, patch structure, and low-rank covariance structure [27, 19, 5]. Modern blind denoisers instead learn this behavior from data, including convolutional, self-supervised, and real-image blind-denoising methods [10, 2, 32]. These works motivate the possibility that an explicit noise or time label may be redundant when the corrupted sample itself contains enough information to infer it.

Blind generative models and intrinsic dimension.

Recent work has extended this question to generative modeling. Kadkhodaie et al. [13] show that blind denoising diffusion models can follow an implicit noise schedule under low intrinsic dimension, building on the view that natural images concentrate near low-dimensional geometric structure [11, 23, 4]. Related perspectives connect denoising to score estimation and empirical Bayes identities [21, 8, 24], and to autonomous or time-unconditional generative dynamics [26, 31]. Our setting differs from these works because flow matching contains an additional ambiguity: even if time is known, the target velocity remains random through the coupling between source and target samples.

Noise conditioning, residual dimension, and coupling in flow matching.

Closest to our motivation, Sun et al. [28] analyze why noise-unconditional denoising and flow-based generative models can remain effective, arguing that the posterior over the hidden noise level concentrates in high ambient dimension. We refine this dimensional picture for low-rank data in flow matching: the identifiable clock lives in the residual noise subspace orthogonal to the data, so the relevant dimension is d−kd-k, not dd alone. This distinction matters when the intrinsic dimension grows with the ambient dimension. In parallel, prior work has shown that flow-matching performance depends strongly on the source–target coupling, with improved couplings based on rectified flows, optimal transport, and minibatch optimal transport [18, 29, 9]. Our contribution is to disentangle these effects: we compare the time-blindness gap against the irreducible coupling variance and show why coupling can remain the dominant lever even when time is hidden.

7 Discussion

Our results show that time conditioning is not always essential in flow matching: in high-dimensional settings, the noisy interpolant can itself reveal the hidden time, because residual noise directions act like an implicit clock. Once time can be inferred from the sample, the dominant source of error is the ambiguity induced by how noise and data are paired, so coupling matter more than explicit time conditioning. This also points toward more powerful time-independent generative models, including equilibrium-style models that learn autonomous dynamics without an externally supplied time variable. Several directions remain open. Our theory identifies one mechanism for time recovery, but it remains to validate which mechanisms trained networks actually use. Future work could probe whether learned models rely on residual noise energy, data-subspace structure, or other implicit time signals. The theory could also be refined beyond the spiked-covariance setting toward nonlinear data geometry, anisotropic covariance, learned representations, or statistics that exploit both residual noise directions and information inside the data subspace.

Proof.

Combining the FM floor with the three-term decomposition immediately gives:

The irreducible time-blind error is at least as large as the FM irreducible error:

minf⁡ℒTB​(f)=𝒞π+Δ≥𝒞π⏟minv⁡ℒFM​(v).\min_{f}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TB}}(f)\;=\;\mathcal{C}_{\pi}+\Delta\;\geq\;\underbrace{\mathcal{C}_{\pi}}_{\min_{v}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(v)}.
