Appendix B Proofs for Section 4: Closing the Two Sources of Irreducible Error

Proposition 1 establishes that the irreducible error of time-blind flow matching is strictly higher than that of FM, raising the natural question of why time-blind models work at all in practice. Extending the analysis of Kadkhodaie et al. [13] from the diffusion setting to linear interpolants, we resolve this puzzle by showing that the interpolation time tt is almost entirely determined by the observation zz alone, so conditioning on tt provides little additional information and the gap Δ=𝔼[Var(𝔼[u∣z,t]∣z)]\Delta=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[u\mid z,t]\mid z)] becomes negligible relative to the irreducible coupling variance 𝒞π\mathcal{C}_{\pi}.

Mechanism: concentration reveals time.

The observation zt=(1−t)​ε+t​xz_{t}=(1-t)\varepsilon+t\,x mixes noise and signal with weights determined by tt. In high dimensions, simple statistics of ztz_{t} (such as its projected norm) concentrate sharply around deterministic functions of tt. If this concentration is sufficiently strong, tt can be recovered from zz alone, so conditioning on tt provides little additional information.

B.1 Baseline Spiked Model and Notation

The headline chain of this appendix, spiked identifiability (Subsection B.2) ⇒\Rightarrow absolute gap bound (Subsection B.5) ⇒\Rightarrow relative cost (Subsection B.7), is built on a single baseline regime that we collect once here for reuse.

Spiked Gaussian model.

The data follow a spiked Gaussian:

x∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ),Σ=Ux​Λ​Ux⊤+σ2​Id,x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma),\qquad\Sigma=U_{x}\Lambda U_{x}^{\top}+\sigma^{2}I_{d}, (11)

where Ux∈ℝd×kU_{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} spans the kk-dimensional signal subspace, Λ=diag⁡(λ1,…,λk)\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{k}) collects the signal variances with λmax:=maxi⁡λi<∞\lambda_{\max}:=\max_{i}\lambda_{i}<\infty, and σ2>0\sigma^{2}>0 gives isotropic residual variance in the orthogonal complement. This is a standard tractable proxy for the broader empirical observation that natural high-dimensional data concentrate near a low-dimensional subspace, used throughout high-dimensional statistics [12] and the theoretical analysis of diffusion models [6, 30]. Because all results are rotationally invariant, we may take Σ\Sigma diagonal in its eigenbasis with per-coordinate variances Si=λiS_{i}=\lambda_{i} for i≤ki\leq k and Si=σ2S_{i}=\sigma^{2} for i>ki>k.

Linear interpolant.

We observe

zt=(1−t)​ε+t​x,ε∼𝒩⁡(0,Id),t∼Unif⁡(I),z_{t}=(1-t)\,\varepsilon+t\,x,\qquad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}),\qquad t\sim\mathrm{Unif}(I), (12)

where I⊂(0,1)I\subset(0,1) is a closed interval avoiding t∗=1/(1+σ2)t^{*}=1/(1+\sigma^{2}).

Noise-subspace statistic.

Let P⟂∈ℝd×dP_{\perp}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} project onto the (d−k)(d-k)-dimensional orthogonal complement of the signal subspace. The key statistic is

σ^⟂2​(z):=1d−k​‖P⟂​z‖2,\widehat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}(z)\;:=\;\frac{1}{d-k}\,\|P_{\perp}z\|^{2}, (13)

which estimates the deterministic noise-subspace variance

σ⟂2​(t):=(1−t)2+t2​σ2.\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t)\;:=\;(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}\sigma^{2}. (14)

We also write ri​(t)=(1−t)2+t2​Sir_{i}(t)=(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}S_{i} for the per-coordinate interpolant variance and αi​(t):=(t​Si−(1−t))/ri​(t)\alpha_{i}(t):=(tS_{i}-(1-t))/r_{i}(t) for the per-coordinate optimal slope.

Noise-subspace time estimator.

Inverting the variance clock σ⟂2\sigma_{\perp}^{2} yields the noise-subspace time estimator used throughout the appendix:

t^​(z):=(σ⟂2)−1​(Πσ⟂2​(I)​(σ^⟂2​(z))),\hat{t}(z)\;:=\;\bigl(\sigma_{\perp}^{2}\bigr)^{-1}\!\Bigl(\Pi_{\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(I)}\!\bigl(\widehat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}(z)\bigr)\Bigr), (15)

where Πσ⟂2​(I)\Pi_{\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(I)} denotes projection onto the closed interval σ⟂2​(I)⊂ℝ\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(I)\subset\mathbb{R}. The projection ensures t^​(z)∈I\hat{t}(z)\in I even when σ^⟂2​(z)\widehat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}(z) leaves the range of σ⟂2\sigma_{\perp}^{2} on II (a positive-probability event, since the underlying chi-square statistic is unbounded), and only sharpens the bounds below since projection cannot increase distance to any point in the interval.

Constants convention.

All implicit constants in the O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) statements that follow depend only on the time interval II, the noise floor σ2\sigma^{2}, and the bounded signal spectrum λmax\lambda_{\max}, not on dd or kk.

B.2 Identifiability under Spiked Covariance

This appendix restates Theorem 2 from the main text in full formal detail and provides the complete proof. Working in the baseline spiked Gaussian model (Subsection B.1), the concentration argument here takes a particularly clean form: projecting onto the noise subspace yields an isotropic Gaussian, so the projected norm follows a standard χd−k2\chi^{2}_{d-k} distribution (up to scaling), and the estimation rate scales with the noise-subspace dimension d−kd-k.

Theorem 2 (Restated). Under the baseline spiked model of Subsection B.1, the estimator

t^​(z)=(σ⟂2)−1​(σ^⟂2​(z))\hat{t}(z)\;=\;(\sigma_{\perp}^{2})^{-1}\!\bigl(\widehat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}(z)\bigr)

satisfies t^​(z)=t+Op​(1/d−k)\hat{t}(z)=t+O_{p}\!\left(1/\sqrt{d-k}\right) for tt bounded away from t∗=1/(1+σ2)t^{*}=1/(1+\sigma^{2}).

Proof.

Write

σ⟂2​(t):=(1−t)2+t2​σ2.\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t):=(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}\sigma^{2}.

We show that the projected noise-subspace variance acts as a high-dimensional clock for the interpolation time. The proof has three steps: projection, concentration, and inversion.

Step 1: Projecting onto the noise subspace produces an isotropic Gaussian clock. Let P⟂P_{\perp} be the orthogonal projector onto the complement of the kk-dimensional signal subspace. Projecting the interpolant gives

P⟂​zt=(1−t)​P⟂​ε+t​P⟂​x.P_{\perp}z_{t}\;=\;(1-t)\,P_{\perp}\varepsilon\;+\;t\,P_{\perp}x.

Under the spiked covariance model,

P⟂​ε∼𝒩⁡(0,Id−k),P⟂​x∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​Id−k),P_{\perp}\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d-k}),\qquad P_{\perp}x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{d-k}),

and these two projected terms are independent. Therefore, conditional on tt,

P⟂​zt∼𝒩⁡(0,σ⟂2​(t)​Id−k).P_{\perp}z_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\bigl(0,\,\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t)\,I_{d-k}\bigr).

Thus

σ^⟂2​(z):=1d−k​‖P⟂​z‖2\widehat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}(z)\;:=\;\frac{1}{d-k}\,\|P_{\perp}z\|^{2}

is the empirical second moment of d−kd-k independent Gaussian coordinates, each with variance σ⟂2​(t)\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t). This projected variance is the statistic from which we recover time.

Step 2: The projected empirical variance concentrates around σ⟂2​(t)\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t). From the Gaussian representation above,

σ^⟂2​(z)​=𝑑​σ⟂2​(t)​Yd−k,Y∼χd−k2.\widehat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}(z)\;\overset{d}{=}\;\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t)\,\frac{Y}{d-k},\qquad Y\sim\chi^{2}_{d-k}.

By standard chi-square concentration,

Yd−k= 1+Op​(1d−k).\frac{Y}{d-k}\;=\;1\;+\;O_{p}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d-k}}\right).

Therefore,

σ^⟂2​(z)=σ⟂2​(t)​(1+Op​(1d−k)).\widehat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}(z)\;=\;\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t)\!\left(1+O_{p}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d-k}}\right)\right).

Since σ⟂2​(t)\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t) is bounded on any compact interval I⊂(0,1)I\subset(0,1), this gives

σ^⟂2​(z)=σ⟂2​(t)+Op​(1d−k).\widehat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}(z)\;=\;\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t)\;+\;O_{p}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d-k}}\right).

Step 3: Inverting the variance clock transfers the rate to tt. The derivative of the variance curve is

dd​t​σ⟂2​(t)=−2​(1−t)+2​t​σ2,\frac{d}{dt}\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t)\;=\;-2(1-t)+2t\sigma^{2},

and vanishes only at t∗=1/(1+σ2)t^{*}=1/(1+\sigma^{2}). Since II is closed and t∗∉It^{*}\notin I, |(σ⟂2)′​(t)||(\sigma_{\perp}^{2})^{\prime}(t)| is bounded below on II, so σ⟂2\sigma_{\perp}^{2} is monotone there and its inverse is Lipschitz on σ⟂2​(I)\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(I). Define

t^​(z):=(σ⟂2)−1​(σ^⟂2​(z)).\hat{t}(z)\;:=\;(\sigma_{\perp}^{2})^{-1}\!\bigl(\widehat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}(z)\bigr).

Since (σ⟂2)−1​(σ⟂2​(t))=t(\sigma_{\perp}^{2})^{-1}\bigl(\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t)\bigr)=t, Lipschitzness of the inverse gives

|t^​(z)−t|≤C​|σ^⟂2​(z)−σ⟂2​(t)|.|\hat{t}(z)-t|\;\leq\;C\,\bigl|\widehat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}(z)-\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t)\bigr|.

Using Step 2,

t^​(z)−t=Op​(1d−k).\hat{t}(z)-t\;=\;O_{p}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d-k}}\right).

Equivalently,

t^​(z)=t+Op​(1d−k).\hat{t}(z)\;=\;t\;+\;O_{p}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d-k}}\right).

This proves the claimed identifiability rate. ∎

B.3 Closed-Form Inversion of the Variance Clock

The proof of Theorem 2 characterizes the estimator t^​(z)=(σ⟂2)−1​(σ^⟂2)\hat{t}(z)=(\sigma_{\perp}^{2})^{-1}(\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}) abstractly via Lipschitzness of the inverse on a compact interval avoiding t∗t^{*}. For the linear interpolant the inversion has a closed form, which is the formula evaluated in all experiments.

Inverting the variance clock.

Expanding (1−t)2(1-t)^{2}, collecting like powers, and applying the quadratic formula:

σ⟂2​(t)\displaystyle\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t) =(1−t)2+t2​σ2\displaystyle\;=\;(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}\sigma^{2}
= 1−2​t+t2+t2​σ2\displaystyle\;=\;1-2t+t^{2}+t^{2}\sigma^{2}
=(1+σ2)​t2−2​t+1,\displaystyle\;=\;(1+\sigma^{2})\,t^{2}-2t+1,
so setting σ⟂2​(t)=σ^⟂2\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t)=\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2} and moving everything to one side gives the standard form (1+σ2)​t2−2​t+(1−σ^⟂2)=0(1+\sigma^{2})\,t^{2}-2t+(1-\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2})=0, whose two roots are
t±\displaystyle t_{\pm} =2±4−4​(1+σ2)​(1−σ^⟂2)2​(1+σ2).\displaystyle\;=\;\frac{2\pm\sqrt{4-4(1+\sigma^{2})(1-\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2})}}{2(1+\sigma^{2})}. (16)
Branch selection.

The clock σ⟂2​(t)\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t) is a strictly convex parabola attaining its global minimum

σ⟂2​(t∗)=σ21+σ2att∗=11+σ2.\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t^{*})\;=\;\frac{\sigma^{2}}{1+\sigma^{2}}\qquad\text{at}\qquad t^{*}\;=\;\frac{1}{1+\sigma^{2}}.

Each value σ^⟂2∈(σ2/(1+σ2), 1]\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}\in(\sigma^{2}/(1+\sigma^{2}),\,1] has two preimages: t−t_{-} on the descending branch [0,t∗][0,t^{*}] and t+t_{+} on the ascending branch [t∗,1][t^{*},1]. On any working interval I⊂[0,t∗]I\subset[0,t^{*}] (the regime used throughout our experiments, where σ2≪1\sigma^{2}\ll 1 pushes t∗t^{*} close to 11) the inverse selects the descending branch, equivalently the minus sign:

t^​(z)=2−4−4​(1+σ2)​(1−σ^⟂2)2​(1+σ2).\hat{t}(z)\;=\;\frac{2-\sqrt{4-4(1+\sigma^{2})(1-\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2})}}{2(1+\sigma^{2})}. (17)

This is the closed-form realization of the inverse (σ⟂2)−1(\sigma_{\perp}^{2})^{-1} used in Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 2.

B.4 Effective-Rank Generalization

The spiked proof above relies on a specific structural fact: projecting onto the noise subspace yields an isotropic Gaussian, so the projected norm ‖z⟂‖2\|z_{\perp}\|^{2} is a standard χd−k2\chi^{2}_{d-k} up to the scalar σ⟂2​(t)\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t). Real data covariances rarely exhibit such a sharp signal/noise split; e.g. the latent covariances of trained VAEs typically decay smoothly over several orders of magnitude. We now show that the same project–concentrate–invert argument carries through for arbitrary PSD Σ\Sigma and any orthogonal projector PP, with the isotropic χd−k2\chi^{2}_{d-k} replaced by a weighted chi-square whose effective sample size is the effective rank of the projected interpolant covariance.

Effective dimension of the observation.

The strength of the concentration argument depends on how many independent directions contribute to the statistic. In the isotropic setting of Appendix B.2, concentration improves with the ambient dimension of the projected subspace, yielding the familiar 1/n1/\sqrt{n} scaling for an nn-dimensional average. In the anisotropic setting, however, different directions contribute unequally, and the relevant notion of dimension is no longer the ambient nn but the effective rank of the underlying covariance: for a PSD matrix A∈ℝn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} with eigenvalues {λi}\{\lambda_{i}\},

reff​(A):=(tr⁡A)2tr⁡(A2)=(∑iλi)2∑iλi2.r_{\mathrm{eff}}(A)\;:=\;\frac{(\operatorname{tr}A)^{2}}{\operatorname{tr}(A^{2})}\;=\;\frac{\bigl(\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\bigr)^{2}}{\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}^{2}}.

Unlike the algebraic rank, the effective rank quantifies how evenly variance is distributed across eigen-directions. When all eigenvalues are equal, reff​(A)=nr_{\mathrm{eff}}(A)=n; in highly anisotropic regimes it can be much smaller, reflecting a collapse onto a few dominant directions. It therefore plays the role of an intrinsic statistical dimension governing concentration rates, replacing the ambient dimension in heterogeneous settings.

Setup.

Let x∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ)x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma) with Σ∈ℝd×d\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} an arbitrary PSD covariance, zt=(1−t)​ε+t​xz_{t}=(1-t)\varepsilon+tx with ε∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), and let PP be an orthogonal projector of rank mm with orthonormal basis Q∈ℝd×mQ\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}. Write ΣP:=Q⊤​Σ​Q\Sigma_{P}:=Q^{\top}\Sigma Q for the induced covariance on range⁡(P)\operatorname{range}(P), μ¯P:=tr⁡(ΣP)/m\bar{\mu}_{P}:=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{P})/m for its spectral mean, and ΣP,t:=(1−t)2​Im+t2​ΣP\Sigma_{P,t}:=(1-t)^{2}I_{m}+t^{2}\Sigma_{P} for the projected interpolant covariance, whose effective rank we denote reff​(P,t):=reff​(ΣP,t)r_{\mathrm{eff}}(P,t):=r_{\mathrm{eff}}(\Sigma_{P,t}). As in the spiked case, the variance-to-time map t↦σt2​(μ¯P):=(1−t)2+t2​μ¯Pt\mapsto\sigma_{t}^{2}(\bar{\mu}_{P}):=(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}\bar{\mu}_{P} has a unique critical point tμ¯P∗:=1/(1+μ¯P)t^{*}_{\bar{\mu}_{P}}:=1/(1+\bar{\mu}_{P}).

Proposition B.1 (Effective-rank identifiability).

Under the setup above, on any closed interval avoiding tμ¯P∗t^{*}_{\bar{\mu}_{P}}, the estimator t^​(z)\hat{t}(z) obtained by inverting σt2​(μ¯P)=‖P​z‖2/m\sigma_{t}^{2}(\bar{\mu}_{P})=\|Pz\|^{2}/m on the relevant branch satisfies

t^(z)=t+Op(reff(P,t)−1/2).\hat{t}(z)\;=\;t\;+\;O_{p}\!\left(r_{\mathrm{eff}}(P,t)^{-1/2}\right).
Proof.

The argument follows the same project–concentrate–invert structure as Theorem 2; only the concentration step changes.

Step 1: Weighted-Gaussian projection. Since P=Q​Q⊤P=QQ^{\top}, ‖P​zt‖2=‖Q⊤​zt‖2\|Pz_{t}\|^{2}=\|Q^{\top}z_{t}\|^{2}, and Q⊤​zt=(1−t)​Q⊤​ε+t​Q⊤​xQ^{\top}z_{t}=(1-t)Q^{\top}\varepsilon+t\,Q^{\top}x with Q⊤​ε∼𝒩⁡(0,Im)Q^{\top}\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{m}) and Q⊤​x∼𝒩⁡(0,ΣP)Q^{\top}x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{P}) independent. Rotating to the eigenbasis of ΣP\Sigma_{P} decomposes Q⊤​ztQ^{\top}z_{t} into independent Gaussian coordinates with per-coordinate variance σt,i2:=(1−t)2+t2​μi\sigma_{t,i}^{2}:=(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}\mu_{i}, where {μi}i=1m\{\mu_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m} are the eigenvalues of ΣP\Sigma_{P}. Writing χ1,i2\chi^{2}_{1,i} for i.i.d. χ12\chi^{2}_{1} variates,

‖P​zt‖2​=𝑑​∑i=1mσt,i2​χ1,i2.\|Pz_{t}\|^{2}\;\overset{d}{=}\;\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sigma_{t,i}^{2}\,\chi^{2}_{1,i}.

This is the spiked Step 1 with weights σt,i2\sigma_{t,i}^{2} in place of a common scalar σ⟂2​(t)\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t), and ΣP,t\Sigma_{P,t} has eigenvalues exactly {σt,i2}i=1m\{\sigma_{t,i}^{2}\}_{i=1}^{m}.

Step 2: Concentration via the effective-rank identity. Let q^:=‖P​z‖2/m\hat{q}:=\|Pz\|^{2}/m. Using 𝔼⁡[χ12]=1\mathbb{E}[\chi^{2}_{1}]=1 and Var⁡(χ12)=2\operatorname{Var}(\chi^{2}_{1})=2,

𝔼⁡[q^]=1m​∑iσt,i2=σt2​(μ¯P),Var⁡(q^)=2m2​∑i(σt,i2)2.\mathbb{E}[\hat{q}]\;=\;\tfrac{1}{m}\sum_{i}\sigma_{t,i}^{2}\;=\;\sigma_{t}^{2}(\bar{\mu}_{P}),\qquad\operatorname{Var}(\hat{q})\;=\;\frac{2}{m^{2}}\sum_{i}(\sigma_{t,i}^{2})^{2}.

Recognising ∑iσt,i2=tr⁡ΣP,t=m​σt2​(μ¯P)\sum_{i}\sigma_{t,i}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{P,t}=m\,\sigma_{t}^{2}(\bar{\mu}_{P}) and ∑i(σt,i2)2=tr⁡(ΣP,t2)\sum_{i}(\sigma_{t,i}^{2})^{2}=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{P,t}^{2}), the definition reff​(P,t)=(tr⁡ΣP,t)2/tr⁡(ΣP,t2)r_{\mathrm{eff}}(P,t)=(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{P,t})^{2}/\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{P,t}^{2}) gives ∑i(σt,i2)2=m2​σt2​(μ¯P)2/reff​(P,t)\sum_{i}(\sigma_{t,i}^{2})^{2}=m^{2}\sigma_{t}^{2}(\bar{\mu}_{P})^{2}/r_{\mathrm{eff}}(P,t), so

Var⁡(q^)=2​σt2​(μ¯P)2reff​(P,t).\operatorname{Var}(\hat{q})\;=\;\frac{2\,\sigma_{t}^{2}(\bar{\mu}_{P})^{2}}{r_{\mathrm{eff}}(P,t)}.

The effective rank acts as an effective sample size for the heteroskedastic average q^\hat{q}: it equals mm when all σt,i2\sigma_{t,i}^{2} are equal and degrades smoothly under spectral anisotropy. Chebyshev’s inequality applied to q^\hat{q} yields

q^​(z)=σt2​(μ¯P)+Op​(σt2​(μ¯P)reff​(P,t)).\hat{q}(z)\;=\;\sigma_{t}^{2}(\bar{\mu}_{P})\;+\;O_{p}\!\left(\frac{\sigma_{t}^{2}(\bar{\mu}_{P})}{\sqrt{r_{\mathrm{eff}}(P,t)}}\right).

This is the only step where the proof diverges from Theorem 2: the textbook χd−k2\chi^{2}_{d-k} rate 1/d−k1/\sqrt{d-k} is replaced by the weighted-chi-square rate 1/reff​(P,t)1/\sqrt{r_{\mathrm{eff}}(P,t)}, with the latter reducing to the former when the weights are constant.

Step 3: Lipschitz inversion. The variance-to-time map t↦σt2​(μ¯P)t\mapsto\sigma_{t}^{2}(\bar{\mu}_{P}) has derivative −2​(1−t)+2​t​μ¯P-2(1-t)+2t\bar{\mu}_{P}, vanishing only at tμ¯P∗t^{*}_{\bar{\mu}_{P}}. On any closed interval II with tμ¯P∗∉It^{*}_{\bar{\mu}_{P}}\notin I, |(σt2​(μ¯P))′||(\sigma_{t}^{2}(\bar{\mu}_{P}))^{\prime}| is bounded below, so the inverse is Lipschitz on σt2​(μ¯P)​(I)\sigma_{t}^{2}(\bar{\mu}_{P})(I) with constant CC depending only on II and μ¯P\bar{\mu}_{P}. The argument from Step 3 of Theorem 2 then gives

|t^(z)−t|≤C|q^(z)−σt2(μ¯P)|=Op(reff(P,t)−1/2),|\hat{t}(z)-t|\;\leq\;C\,\bigl|\hat{q}(z)-\sigma_{t}^{2}(\bar{\mu}_{P})\bigr|\;=\;O_{p}\!\left(r_{\mathrm{eff}}(P,t)^{-1/2}\right),

which is the claimed rate. ∎

Corollary B.2 (Spiked recovery).

Theorem 2 is the case of Proposition B.1 with Σ=Ux​Λ​Ux⊤+σ2​Id\Sigma=U_{x}\Lambda U_{x}^{\top}+\sigma^{2}I_{d} and P=P⟂P=P_{\perp}.

Proof.

Under the spiked covariance and P=P⟂P=P_{\perp}, P⟂​Ux=0P_{\perp}U_{x}=0, so the induced covariance collapses to the isotropic residual ΣP=σ2​Id−k\Sigma_{P}=\sigma^{2}I_{d-k}. All eigenvalues μi\mu_{i} equal σ2\sigma^{2}, so μ¯P=σ2\bar{\mu}_{P}=\sigma^{2}, tμ¯P∗=1/(1+σ2)=t∗t^{*}_{\bar{\mu}_{P}}=1/(1+\sigma^{2})=t^{*}, and ΣP,t=σ⟂2​(t)​Id−k\Sigma_{P,t}=\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t)\,I_{d-k}. Constant eigenvalues give reff​(P,t)=(d−k)2/(d−k)=d−kr_{\mathrm{eff}}(P,t)=(d-k)^{2}/(d-k)=d-k, and the Proposition’s rate becomes the Op​(1/d−k)O_{p}(1/\sqrt{d-k}) bound of Theorem 2. ∎

Scope of the spiked model in the rest of the paper.

Proposition B.1 establishes that the identifiability mechanism is not specific to isotropic residuals; the spiked model provides the cleanest closed-form constants but no essential structure. The remainder of the paper retains the spiked model for two distinct reasons. First, the propagation from identifiability to the time-blindness gap Δ\Delta (Section B.5) requires closed-form per-coordinate fourth-moment calculations that the spiked structure makes available; the corresponding anisotropic calculation introduces additional weighted-moment bookkeeping without changing the qualitative conclusion that Δ/𝒞π\Delta/\mathcal{C}_{\pi} vanishes with the residual-subspace dimension. Second, the empirical predictor in Section 5.2 uses the spiked-derived 1/d−k1/\sqrt{d-k} rate because it has a single interpretable parameter (kk at a fixed explained-variance threshold) that we report transparently per dataset, and the empirical fit on VAE latents with visibly anisotropic spectra (Figure 5) shows the spiked prediction is already tight without the effective-rank refinement. Proposition B.1 is therefore best read as a robustness statement about the identifiability mechanism, not as a competing predictor or an empirical hypothesis.

B.5 Absolute Bound on the Time-Blindness Gap

Proposition B.3 (Absolute time-blindness gap bound).

Under the spiked covariance model with t∼Unif⁡(I)t\sim\mathrm{Unif}(I),

Δ=O⁡(dd−k),\Delta\;=\;O\!\left(\frac{d}{d-k}\right), (18)

where Δ:=𝔼z[Vart|z(𝔼[u∣z,t])]\Delta:=\mathbb{E}_{z}\!\left[\mathrm{Var}_{t\mid z}\!\big(\mathbb{E}[u\mid z,t]\big)\right].

Proof.

Let

m:=d−k,q⁡(t):=σ⟂2​(t)=(1−t)2+t2​σ2,q^​(z):=‖P⟂​z‖2m.m\;:=\;d-k,\qquad q(t)\;:=\;\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t)\;=\;(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}\sigma^{2},\qquad\widehat{q}(z)\;:=\;\frac{\|P_{\perp}z\|^{2}}{m}.

The proof has two steps. First, we upper-bound the time-blindness gap by the error of a concrete time-blind predictor that estimates tt from zz (a brief inverse-clock argument turns this into the error of the noise-subspace variance estimate q^\widehat{q}). Second, we bound the resulting weighted variance-estimation error.

Step 1: Reduce the gap to time-estimation error. Recall that

Δ=𝔼⁡[‖v∗​(z,t)−𝔼⁡[v∗​(z,t)∣z]‖2],\Delta\;=\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\bigl\|v^{*}(z,t)-\mathbb{E}[v^{*}(z,t)\mid z]\bigr\|^{2}\right],

where v∗(z,t)=𝔼[u∣z,t]v^{*}(z,t)=\mathbb{E}[u\mid z,t] is the optimal time-aware predictor.

The conditional expectation 𝔼​[v∗​(z,t)∣z]\mathbb{E}[v^{*}(z,t)\mid z] is the best predictor of v∗​(z,t)v^{*}(z,t) among predictors that only depend on zz. Therefore, for any such predictor g⁡(z)g(z),

Δ≤𝔼⁡[‖v∗​(z,t)−g⁡(z)‖2].\Delta\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|v^{*}(z,t)-g(z)\|^{2}\right].

We use the particular predictor

g⁡(z):=v∗​(z,t^​(z)),g(z)\;:=\;v^{*}(z,\hat{t}(z)),

where t^​(z)∈I\hat{t}(z)\in I is the time estimate constructed in Step 2. This gives

Δ≤𝔼⁡[‖v∗​(z,t)−v∗​(z,t^​(z))‖2].\Delta\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|v^{*}(z,t)-v^{*}(z,\hat{t}(z))\|^{2}\right].

It remains to control how much v∗​(z,t)v^{*}(z,t) changes when tt is replaced by t^​(z)\hat{t}(z). In the diagonal Gaussian model,

vi∗​(z,t)=αi​(t)​zi,αi​(t)=t​Si−(1−t)(1−t)2+t2​Si.v^{*}_{i}(z,t)\;=\;\alpha_{i}(t)\,z_{i},\qquad\alpha_{i}(t)\;=\;\frac{tS_{i}-(1-t)}{(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}S_{i}}.

On II, the functions αi\alpha_{i} are uniformly Lipschitz across all coordinates, since Si∈[σ2,λmax]S_{i}\in[\sigma^{2},\lambda_{\max}] and the denominator is bounded away from zero. Thus there is a constant L=L⁡(I,σ2,λmax)L=L(I,\sigma^{2},\lambda_{\max}) such that

|αi​(t)−αi​(s)|≤L​|t−s|for all ​i​ and ​s,t∈I.|\alpha_{i}(t)-\alpha_{i}(s)|\;\leq\;L\,|t-s|\qquad\text{for all }i\text{ and }s,t\in I.

Therefore,

‖v∗​(z,t)−v∗​(z,s)‖2=∑i=1d(αi​(t)−αi​(s))2​zi2≤L2​‖z‖2​(t−s)2.\|v^{*}(z,t)-v^{*}(z,s)\|^{2}\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{d}\bigl(\alpha_{i}(t)-\alpha_{i}(s)\bigr)^{2}z_{i}^{2}\;\leq\;L^{2}\,\|z\|^{2}\,(t-s)^{2}.

Taking s=t^​(z)s=\hat{t}(z) yields

Δ≤L2​𝔼​[‖z‖2​(t^​(z)−t)2].\Delta\;\leq\;L^{2}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|z\|^{2}\,(\hat{t}(z)-t)^{2}\right]. (19)

Since II is closed and t∗=1/(1+σ2)∉It^{*}=1/(1+\sigma^{2})\notin I, |q′​(t)||q^{\prime}(t)| is bounded below on II, so q−1q^{-1} is Lipschitz on q⁡(I)q(I). Apply this with t^​(z)\hat{t}(z) from (15): since projection onto q⁡(I)q(I) cannot increase distance to q⁡(t)∈q⁡(I)q(t)\in q(I), there is a constant C=C⁡(I,σ2)C=C(I,\sigma^{2}) such that

|t^​(z)−t|≤C​|q^​(z)−q⁡(t)|.|\hat{t}(z)-t|\;\leq\;C\,|\widehat{q}(z)-q(t)|.

Therefore

𝔼⁡[‖z‖2​(t^​(z)−t)2]≤C2​𝔼​[‖z‖2​(q^​(z)−q⁡(t))2].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|z\|^{2}(\hat{t}(z)-t)^{2}\right]\;\leq\;C^{2}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|z\|^{2}(\widehat{q}(z)-q(t))^{2}\right]. (20)

Step 2: Bound the weighted variance-estimation error. Condition on tt. In the noise subspace,

P⟂​zt∼𝒩⁡(0,q⁡(t)​Im),P_{\perp}z_{t}\;\sim\;\mathcal{N}(0,q(t)I_{m}),

so

q^=q⁡(t)​Ym,Y∼χm2.\widehat{q}\;=\;q(t)\,\frac{Y}{m},\qquad Y\sim\chi^{2}_{m}.

For readability, write q:=q⁡(t)q:=q(t), so

q^−q=qm​(Y−m).\widehat{q}-q\;=\;\frac{q}{m}(Y-m).

Split the energy into signal and noise components:

‖z‖2=‖Px​z‖2+‖P⟂​z‖2.\|z\|^{2}\;=\;\|P_{x}z\|^{2}+\|P_{\perp}z\|^{2}.

We bound the two resulting terms separately.

For the signal component, q^\widehat{q} depends only on P⟂​zP_{\perp}z, and under the diagonal spiked Gaussian model with independent ε,x\varepsilon,x, the projected blocks Px​zP_{x}z and P⟂​zP_{\perp}z are independent conditional on tt. Hence

𝔼⁡[‖Px​z‖2​(q^−q)2∣t]=𝔼⁡[‖Px​z‖2∣t]⋅𝔼⁡[(q^−q)2∣t].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|P_{x}z\|^{2}(\widehat{q}-q)^{2}\mid t\right]\;=\;\mathbb{E}[\|P_{x}z\|^{2}\mid t]\cdot\mathbb{E}[(\widehat{q}-q)^{2}\mid t].

The first factor is O⁡(k)O(k), since the kk signal coordinates have uniformly bounded variance on II. The second factor is

𝔼⁡[(q^−q)2∣t]=q2​Var​(Y/m)=2​q2m=O⁡(1m),\mathbb{E}[(\widehat{q}-q)^{2}\mid t]\;=\;q^{2}\,\mathrm{Var}(Y/m)\;=\;\frac{2q^{2}}{m}\;=\;O\!\left(\frac{1}{m}\right),

because q⁡(t)q(t) is bounded on II. Therefore,

𝔼⁡[‖Px​z‖2​(q^−q)2∣t]=O⁡(km).\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|P_{x}z\|^{2}(\widehat{q}-q)^{2}\mid t\right]\;=\;O\!\left(\frac{k}{m}\right).

For the noise component, use

‖P⟂​z‖2=q​Y,q^−q=qm​(Y−m).\|P_{\perp}z\|^{2}\;=\;q\,Y,\qquad\widehat{q}-q\;=\;\frac{q}{m}(Y-m).

Then

𝔼⁡[‖P⟂​z‖2​(q^−q)2∣t]=q3m2​𝔼​[Y​(Y−m)2].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|P_{\perp}z\|^{2}(\widehat{q}-q)^{2}\mid t\right]\;=\;\frac{q^{3}}{m^{2}}\,\mathbb{E}[Y(Y-m)^{2}].

By standard chi-square moment bounds,11 1 Indeed, for Y∼χm2Y\sim\chi^{2}_{m}, 𝔼⁡[(Y−m)2]=2​m\mathbb{E}[(Y-m)^{2}]=2m and 𝔼⁡[(Y−m)3]=8​m\mathbb{E}[(Y-m)^{3}]=8m, so 𝔼⁡[Y​(Y−m)2]=2​m2+8​m\mathbb{E}[Y(Y-m)^{2}]=2m^{2}+8m.

𝔼⁡[Y​(Y−m)2]=O⁡(m2).\mathbb{E}[Y(Y-m)^{2}]\;=\;O(m^{2}).

Since q⁡(t)q(t) is uniformly bounded on II, the noise contribution is

𝔼⁡[‖P⟂​z‖2​(q^−q)2∣t]=O⁡(1).\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|P_{\perp}z\|^{2}(\widehat{q}-q)^{2}\mid t\right]\;=\;O(1).

Combining the signal and noise contributions,

𝔼⁡[‖z‖2​(q^−q)2∣t]=O⁡(km)+O⁡(1)=O⁡(1+km)=O⁡(dd−k).\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|z\|^{2}(\widehat{q}-q)^{2}\mid t\right]\;=\;O\!\left(\frac{k}{m}\right)+O(1)\;=\;O\!\left(1+\frac{k}{m}\right)\;=\;O\!\left(\frac{d}{d-k}\right).

The bound is uniform over t∈It\in I, so averaging over t∼Unif⁡(I)t\sim\mathrm{Unif}(I) gives

𝔼⁡[‖z‖2​(q^​(z)−q⁡(t))2]=O⁡(dd−k).\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|z\|^{2}(\widehat{q}(z)-q(t))^{2}\right]\;=\;O\!\left(\frac{d}{d-k}\right).

Combining this with (19) and (20) proves Δ=O⁡(d/(d−k))\Delta=O(d/(d-k)). ∎

B.6 Independent Coupling Has Extensive Variance

The coupling variance 𝒞π\mathcal{C}_{\pi} is the irreducible regression floor of (time-conditioned) flow matching: it is paid by even the optimal time-aware predictor and depends only on the choice of coupling π\pi (Lemma A.1). Under independent coupling and the baseline spiked Gaussian model (Subsection B.1), 𝒞π\mathcal{C}_{\pi} scales linearly with the ambient dimension; the proof reduces to a per-coordinate Gaussian closed form.

Proposition B.4 (Independent coupling has extensive variance).

Under the spiked Gaussian model with independent coupling and t∼Unif⁡(I)t\sim\mathrm{Unif}(I),

𝒞π=Ω⁡(d).\mathcal{C}_{\pi}\;=\;\Omega(d).
Proof.

Coordinate reduction. Recall that, working in the eigenbasis of Σ\Sigma, we write

xi∼𝒩⁡(0,Si),x_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,S_{i}),

where SiS_{i} denotes the ii-th eigenvalue of the data covariance Σ\Sigma. Under the spiked model,

Si={λi+σ2,i≤k,σ2,i>k.S_{i}=\begin{cases}\lambda_{i}+\sigma^{2},&i\leq k,\\ \sigma^{2},&i>k.\end{cases}

Because the independent coupling makes xx and ε\varepsilon independent, and because both are diagonal in this basis, the coordinates decouple. Hence it suffices to compute the one-dimensional conditional variance and then sum over coordinates.

Gaussian conditioning. Fix a coordinate ii. Conditional on tt, the pair

ui=xi−εi,zi=(1−t)​εi+t​xiu_{i}=x_{i}-\varepsilon_{i},\qquad z_{i}=(1-t)\varepsilon_{i}+tx_{i}

is jointly Gaussian. Since xi∼𝒩⁡(0,Si)x_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,S_{i}) and εi∼𝒩⁡(0,1)\varepsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) are independent,

Var⁡(ui∣t)=Si+1,\operatorname{Var}(u_{i}\mid t)=S_{i}+1,
Var⁡(zi∣t)=(1−t)2+t2​Si,\operatorname{Var}(z_{i}\mid t)=(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}S_{i},

and

Cov⁡(ui,zi∣t)=Cov⁡(xi−εi,(1−t)​εi+t​xi)=t​Si−(1−t).\operatorname{Cov}(u_{i},z_{i}\mid t)=\operatorname{Cov}(x_{i}-\varepsilon_{i},(1-t)\varepsilon_{i}+tx_{i})=tS_{i}-(1-t).

Since (ui,zi)(u_{i},z_{i}) is jointly Gaussian conditional on tt, the scalar Gaussian conditioning formula gives

Var⁡(ui∣zi,t)=Var⁡(ui∣t)−Cov⁡(ui,zi∣t)2Var⁡(zi∣t).\operatorname{Var}(u_{i}\mid z_{i},t)=\operatorname{Var}(u_{i}\mid t)-\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(u_{i},z_{i}\mid t)^{2}}{\operatorname{Var}(z_{i}\mid t)}.

Substituting the above expressions gives

Var⁡(ui∣zi,t)=(Si+1)−(t​Si−(1−t))2(1−t)2+t2​Si.\operatorname{Var}(u_{i}\mid z_{i},t)=(S_{i}+1)-\frac{(tS_{i}-(1-t))^{2}}{(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}S_{i}}.

A direct simplification yields

Var⁡(ui∣zi,t)=Si(1−t)2+t2​Si.\operatorname{Var}(u_{i}\mid z_{i},t)=\frac{S_{i}}{(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}S_{i}}.

Uniform lower bound and summation. Since S↦S/((1−t)2+t2​S)S\mapsto S/((1-t)^{2}+t^{2}S) is increasing for each fixed t∈It\in I, and since Si≥σ2>0S_{i}\geq\sigma^{2}>0, we have

Si(1−t)2+t2​Si≥σ2(1−t)2+t2​σ2.\frac{S_{i}}{(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}S_{i}}\geq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}\sigma^{2}}.

Because I⊂(0,1)I\subset(0,1) is closed and bounded, the right-hand side has a positive minimum on II. Define

c0:=mint∈I⁡σ2(1−t)2+t2​σ2>0.c_{0}:=\min_{t\in I}\frac{\sigma^{2}}{(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}\sigma^{2}}>0.

Therefore, uniformly over all coordinates ii and all t∈It\in I,

Var⁡(ui∣zi,t)≥c0.\operatorname{Var}(u_{i}\mid z_{i},t)\geq c_{0}.

Thus,

𝒞π=∑i=1d𝔼t​[Var⁡(ui∣zi,t)]≥∑i=1dc0=c0​d.\mathcal{C}_{\pi}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[\operatorname{Var}(u_{i}\mid z_{i},t)\right]\geq\sum_{i=1}^{d}c_{0}=c_{0}d.

Hence 𝒞π=Ω⁡(d)\mathcal{C}_{\pi}=\Omega(d).

∎

B.7 Relative Cost of Time-Independence

Combining the two preceding propositions: the time-blindness gap Δ\Delta is bounded relative to the coupling variance 𝒞π\mathcal{C}_{\pi} by O⁡(1/(d−k))O(1/(d-k)). This is the headline result, equivalent to Theorem 3 in the main text.

Theorem B.5 (Relative cost of time-independence).

Under the spiked Gaussian model with independent coupling and t∼Unif⁡(I)t\sim\mathrm{Unif}(I),

Δ𝒞π=O⁡(1d−k).\frac{\Delta}{\mathcal{C}_{\pi}}\;=\;O\!\left(\frac{1}{d-k}\right). (21)

In particular, holding kk and the spectral parameters fixed, the ratio is O⁡(1/d)O(1/d).

Proof.

By Proposition B.3, there is a constant C1=C1​(I,σ2,λmax)C_{1}=C_{1}(I,\sigma^{2},\lambda_{\max}) such that

Δ≤C1​dd−k.\Delta\;\leq\;C_{1}\,\frac{d}{d-k}.

By Proposition B.4, 𝒞π≥c0​d\mathcal{C}_{\pi}\geq c_{0}\,d for a constant c0=c0​(I,σ2,λmax)>0c_{0}=c_{0}(I,\sigma^{2},\lambda_{\max})>0. Dividing,

Δ𝒞π≤C1​d/(d−k)c0​d=C1/c0d−k=O⁡(1d−k),\frac{\Delta}{\mathcal{C}_{\pi}}\;\leq\;\frac{C_{1}\,d/(d-k)}{c_{0}\,d}\;=\;\frac{C_{1}/c_{0}}{d-k}\;=\;O\!\left(\frac{1}{d-k}\right),

where the dd factor in the numerator and denominator cancels, leaving the rate determined entirely by the noise-subspace dimension d−kd-k. ∎

The bound is constructive: Proposition B.3 upper-bounds the optimal time-blind predictor by exhibiting one specific g∗g^{*} that uses the noise-subspace estimator; the actual optimum v¯​(z)=𝔼​[u∣z]\bar{v}(z)=\mathbb{E}[u\mid z] can only do better. The ambient dimension dd enters only through the energy normalization 𝔼⁡[‖z‖2]=Θ⁡(d)\mathbb{E}[\|z\|^{2}]=\Theta(d) on both sides of the ratio and cancels; the statistical content is the O⁡(1/(d−k))O(1/(d-k)) rate, controlled by the noise-subspace dimension alone. Holding kk fixed and varying dd gives the O⁡(1/d)O(1/d) ratio scaling; holding d−kd-k fixed and varying kk leaves the ratio bounded by a constant, the prediction that pulls the bound apart from the per-dimension account of Sun et al. [28] (Section 6). Note that the absolute gap Δ=O⁡(d/(d−k))\Delta=O(d/(d-k)) does not itself vanish when d−kd-k is comparable to dd: it remains O⁡(1)O(1), and what vanishes is the ratio. Methods that suppress the coupling variance directly (optimal transport, mini-batch OT, rectified flows; Section 4.2) drive the dominant Term II down, leaving Δ\Delta as the only remaining residual.

Appendix C Experimental Details

C.1 Datasets and Architectures

Our experiments cover three datasets with two distinct backbones. CIFAR-10 is modeled in pixel space with an ADM UNet; CelebA-HQ and FFHQ are modeled in the latent space of a pretrained VAE using a SiT transformer. We document each setup below; later experiment subsections reference the relevant setup rather than redefining it.

Backbones.

For CIFAR-10 we use an ADM UNet [7] with 128128 base channels, channel multipliers [1,2,2,2][1,2,2,2], 22 residual blocks per resolution, multi-head attention at 16×1616\times 16 resolution (44 heads, 6464 channels per head), and dropout 0.10.1, totaling approximately 35.735.7M parameters. For CelebA-HQ and FFHQ we use SiT-B/2: a transformer of depth 1212, hidden size 768768, 1212 attention heads, and patch size 22, acting on 16×16=25616\times 16=256 tokens after encoding 256×256256\times 256 images to 4×32×324\times 32\times 32 latents with the Stable Diffusion 1.5 VAE (stabilityai/sd-vae-ft-ema, latents cached once before training).

C.2 Loss Decomposition Validation

Setup.

We train four flow matching models per dataset in a 2×22\times 2 factorial design, varying time conditioning (on/off) and coupling (independent/OT), on CIFAR-10, CelebA-HQ, and FFHQ. Within each dataset, all four variants share the identical architecture and hyperparameters; the only differences are (i) whether the coupling is independent or mini-batch OT (exact EMD pot_emd) and (ii) whether the model conditions on tt or receives t=0t=0 at every step. The “time-blind” variant zeros the time input fed to the network at every step while keeping the time-embedding layers in the architecture, so the parameter count is identical across all four models. Per-dataset architectures, preprocessing, and training hyperparameters are specified in Appendix C.1; we summarize the cells below.

CIFAR-10.

Pixel-space ADM UNet (Table C.1) trained for 200,000200{,}000 steps with per-GPU batch size 128128. OT coupling uses exact EMD with B=128B=128.

CelebA-HQ.

SiT-B/2 in the Stable Diffusion VAE latent space (Table C.1) trained for 100,000100{,}000 steps with global batch size 256256. OT coupling uses exact EMD with B=256B=256.

FFHQ.

SiT-B/2 in the Stable Diffusion VAE latent space (Table C.1), with the same protocol as CelebA-HQ: 100,000100{,}000 steps, global batch size 256256, exact EMD with B=256B=256.

MSE evaluation protocol.

We compute the mean MSE under EMA weights in eval mode as a measurement of the converged training-loss floor of each cell. The measured quantity is the irreducible loss floor of the training distribution: a property of the joint distribution over (x,ε,t)(x,\varepsilon,t), not a generalization claim. To ensure a fair comparison, each model is evaluated under the coupling it was trained with: OT models (A, C) are evaluated with the same pot_emd permutation applied per eval batch (using the BB matching training), while independent models (B, D) use random pairing.

CIFAR-10. CIFAR-10 has an official train/test partition (inherited from its classification-dataset origin), so we evaluate on its 10,00010{,}000-image test split (78 batches of 128 samples). The train-vs-test loss gap is ≤0.0015\leq 0.0015, well within the per-batch standard error, so this distinction does not affect the decomposition.

CelebA-HQ and FFHQ. These benchmarks are introduced in the literature as generative-model benchmarks without a canonical train/test partition [14, 15], so following the convention of those benchmarks we evaluate on the same VAE-latent image set used for training, with fresh Gaussian noise ε∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and uniform t∼𝒰⁡[0,1]t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1] drawn for each batch (78 batches of 256 samples).

FID evaluation protocol.

For each of the four cells per dataset we generate 50,00050{,}000 samples by integrating the trained vector field with 250250 Euler steps from t=0t=0 to t=1t=1 using the EMA weights, and report clean-FID [22]. All four cells (A, B, C, D) per dataset use the identical sampler, sample count, and reference set; the only differences across cells are the model weights themselves. Per-dataset scoring details follow.

CIFAR-10. Samples are scored directly in pixel space against the standard CIFAR-10 training-set reference statistics.

CelebA-HQ and FFHQ. Samples are produced in VAE-latent space and decoded back to 256×256256\times 256 pixels with the same stabilityai/sd-vae-ft-ema VAE used at training time before scoring against each dataset’s full real distribution as the reference, following the convention of those benchmarks [14, 15].

Results.

Converged loss-floor values for all three datasets are reported in Table C.2. On CIFAR-10, the coupling effect is δcoupling=0.025\delta_{\text{coupling}}=0.025 regardless of time conditioning, and the time-blindness effect is δtime=0.001\delta_{\text{time}}=0.001. On CelebA-HQ, the coupling effect is δcoupling=0.038\delta_{\text{coupling}}=0.038–0.0440.044 and the time-blindness effect is δtime=0.008\delta_{\text{time}}=0.008–0.0140.014. On FFHQ, the coupling effect is δcoupling=0.037\delta_{\text{coupling}}=0.037–0.0380.038 and the time-blindness effect is δtime=0.003\delta_{\text{time}}=0.003–0.0040.004. In all cases the coupling variance dominates and the decomposition is approximately additive.

C.3 Empirical Validation of Time Identifiability

We validate the theoretical predictions of Theorem 2 in four settings: (i) a fully synthetic spiked covariance model where all parameters are controlled exactly, and (ii–iv) real datasets (CIFAR-10 in pixel space, d=3072d=3072; FFHQ and CelebA-HQ in VAE latent space, d=4096d=4096), where the spiked covariance is fitted via PCA and used only for the theoretical prediction, not for data generation.

C.3.1 Common Estimator

In both settings, we observe interpolants of the form zi=(1−ti)​εi+ti​xiz_{i}=(1-t_{i})\,\varepsilon_{i}+t_{i}\,x_{i}, where εi∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)\varepsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) is the source noise and xix_{i} is drawn from a distribution with covariance Σ=Ux​Λ​Ux⊤+σ2​Id\Sigma=U_{x}\Lambda U_{x}^{\top}+\sigma^{2}I_{d}. The interpolation times are sampled as ti∼Uniform⁡[0,1]t_{i}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[0,1] over the full path; we report the mean absolute error MAE:=1N​∑i|t^i−ti|\mathrm{MAE}:=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}|\hat{t}_{i}-t_{i}|, which absorbs both the in-regime (t<t∗t<t^{*}) error and any branch-mismatch contribution near the right endpoint.

Estimator.

Given ziz_{i} alone, we estimate tit_{i} via the noise-subspace statistic. Let U⟂∈ℝd×(d−k)U_{\perp}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times(d-k)} span the orthogonal complement of the signal subspace spanned by UxU_{x}, let P⟂:=U⟂​U⟂⊤P_{\perp}:=U_{\perp}U_{\perp}^{\top} denote the orthogonal projector onto the noise subspace, and define

σ^⟂2:=1d−k​‖P⟂​zi‖2.\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}\;:=\;\frac{1}{d-k}\,\|P_{\perp}z_{i}\|^{2}.

In the noise subspace, the interpolant has variance σ⟂2​(ti):=(1−ti)2+ti2​σ2\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t_{i}):=(1-t_{i})^{2}+t_{i}^{2}\,\sigma^{2}, so σ^⟂2\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2} concentrates around this deterministic function of tit_{i}.

C.3.2 Discarded Samples

We compute t^i\hat{t}_{i} via the closed-form inversion (17) derived in Appendix B.3. The descending-branch minus sign applies in all four settings: Table C.3 reports per-dataset σ⟂2\sigma_{\perp}^{2} and t∗t^{*}, with t∗≥0.89t^{*}\geq 0.89 throughout, so the descending branch covers nearly the full [0,1][0,1] sampling range. The only finite-sample wrinkle is the discriminant, which can become negative. A short rearrangement of the discriminant in (16) gives

4−4​(1+σ2)​(1−σ^⟂2)= 4​[(1+σ2)​σ^⟂2−σ2],4-4(1+\sigma^{2})(1-\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2})\;=\;4\bigl[(1+\sigma^{2})\,\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}-\sigma^{2}\bigr],

which is negative precisely when σ^⟂2<σ2/(1+σ2)=σ⟂2​(t∗)\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}<\sigma^{2}/(1+\sigma^{2})=\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t^{*}), i.e. when the empirical noise-subspace variance falls below the global minimum of the clock and therefore lies outside the range of σ⟂2\sigma_{\perp}^{2}. This can only occur as a finite-sample fluctuation: the chi-square statistic in (22) occasionally dips below its mean far enough to push the estimate into the unattainable region. We discard such samples; in practice fewer than 0.1%0.1\% are affected.

C.3.3 Theoretical Prediction

The proof of Theorem 2 establishes the rate t^−t=Op​(1/d−k)\hat{t}-t=O_{p}(1/\sqrt{d-k}) via Chebyshev’s inequality, but for direct comparison with experiments we want a quantitative reference distribution rather than just a rate. We derive one below in three short moves: the exact variance of the noise-subspace statistic, its propagation through the inverse map, and the aggregation across sampled times.

Variance of the clock statistic.

Conditioned on tit_{i}, the components of U⟂⊤​ziU_{\perp}^{\top}z_{i} are i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,σ⟂2​(ti))\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t_{i})), so (d−k)​σ^⟂2/σ⟂2​(ti)∼χd−k2(d-k)\,\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}/\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t_{i})\sim\chi^{2}_{d-k}. The variance of the chi-square distribution then gives the exact conditional variance

Var⁡(σ^⟂2∣ti)=σ⟂4​(ti)⋅2d−k.\mathrm{Var}\!\bigl(\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}\mid t_{i}\bigr)\;=\;\sigma_{\perp}^{4}(t_{i})\cdot\frac{2}{d-k}. (22)

For large d−kd-k, the central limit theorem additionally implies σ^⟂2\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2} is approximately Gaussian. Equation (22) is the only stochastic input we need; everything that follows propagates it deterministically through the inverse map.

Delta-method propagation to time.

Let g:=(σ⟂2)−1g:=(\sigma_{\perp}^{2})^{-1} denote the inverse map sending σ^⟂2\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2} to t^i\hat{t}_{i}. Its derivative at the true variance is

g′​(σ⟂2​(ti))=1σ˙⟂2​(ti),σ˙⟂2​(t)=−2​(1−t)+2​t​σ2.g^{\prime}\!\bigl(\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t_{i})\bigr)\;=\;\frac{1}{\dot{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}(t_{i})},\qquad\dot{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}(t)\;=\;-2(1-t)+2t\sigma^{2}.

A first-order Taylor expansion of gg around σ⟂2​(ti)\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t_{i}) gives the standard delta-method approximation

t^i−ti≈g′​(σ⟂2​(ti))⋅(σ^⟂2−σ⟂2​(ti)),\hat{t}_{i}-t_{i}\;\approx\;g^{\prime}\!\bigl(\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t_{i})\bigr)\cdot\bigl(\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}-\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t_{i})\bigr),

and squaring then taking variances yields

Var⁡(t^i−ti∣ti)≈1[−2​(1−ti)+2​ti​σ2]2⏟[g′​(σ⟂2​(ti))]2⋅σ⟂4​(ti)⋅2d−k⏟Var⁡(σ^⟂2∣ti).\mathrm{Var}\!\bigl(\hat{t}_{i}-t_{i}\mid t_{i}\bigr)\;\approx\;\underbrace{\frac{1}{\bigl[-2(1-t_{i})+2t_{i}\sigma^{2}\bigr]^{2}}}_{\bigl[g^{\prime}(\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t_{i}))\bigr]^{2}}\cdot\underbrace{\sigma_{\perp}^{4}(t_{i})\cdot\frac{2}{d-k}}_{\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}\mid t_{i})}. (23)

Because gg is a smooth map applied to a CLT-regime statistic, t^i−ti\hat{t}_{i}-t_{i} inherits the Gaussian approximation of σ^⟂2\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2} to leading order. This is the per-sample reference distribution we will compare against the empirical estimator.

Dataset-level prediction.

To produce a single reference curve per dataset, we average (23) over the NN sampled times {ti}i=1N\{t_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}, excluding samples within 0.050.05 of the critical point tcrit=1/(1+σ2)t_{\mathrm{crit}}=1/(1+\sigma^{2}) (where g′g^{\prime} nearly vanishes and the first-order Taylor expansion breaks down). This yields the dataset-level standard deviation

σ¯theory=1N​∑i=1NVar⁡(t^i−ti∣ti),\bar{\sigma}_{\mathrm{theory}}\;=\;\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{Var}\!\bigl(\hat{t}_{i}-t_{i}\mid t_{i}\bigr)}, (24)

and we plot 𝒩⁡(0,σ¯theory2)\mathcal{N}(0,\bar{\sigma}_{\mathrm{theory}}^{2}) against the empirical histogram of t^i−ti\hat{t}_{i}-t_{i}. Equation (24) is the prediction tested in Figure 5.

C.3.4 Setting 1: Synthetic Spiked Covariance

We sample N=10,000N=10{,}000 independent triples (εi,xi,ti)(\varepsilon_{i},x_{i},t_{i}) with εi∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)\varepsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), xi∼𝒩⁡(0,Ux​Λ​Ux⊤+σ2​Id)x_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,U_{x}\Lambda U_{x}^{\top}+\sigma^{2}I_{d}), and ti∼Uniform⁡[0,1]t_{i}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[0,1]. Here Ux∈ℝd×kU_{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} is a random orthonormal basis (obtained via QR decomposition of a Gaussian random matrix), Λ=diag⁡(λ1,…,λk)\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{k}) with eigenvalues spaced linearly between 1.01.0 and 10.010.0, and σ2=0.1\sigma^{2}=0.1.

To verify the 1/d−k1/\sqrt{d-k} scaling, we fix k=10k=10 and sweep the ambient dimension across d∈{20,50,100,200,500,1000}d\in\{20,50,100,200,500,1000\}, giving noise subspace dimensions d−k∈{10,40,90,190,490,990}d-k\in\{10,40,90,190,490,990\}. For each dd, we compute t^i\hat{t}_{i} for all NN samples and record the empirical standard deviation of t^i−ti\hat{t}_{i}-t_{i}.

Results (Figure 5, panels a–b).

Panel (a) shows the empirical standard deviation versus d−kd-k alongside the theoretical prediction; the two curves are nearly indistinguishable, confirming that the delta method approximation is tight. Panel (b) shows the full distribution of estimation errors for the setting k=10k=10, d−k=990d-k=990: the empirical KDE closely tracks the theoretical Gaussian 𝒩⁡(0,σ¯theory2)\mathcal{N}(0,\bar{\sigma}^{2}_{\mathrm{theory}}), with the empirical distribution being slightly more concentrated than the theoretical prediction. This is expected, as the theoretical variance is a first-order upper approximation and the actual estimator benefits from higher-order concentration.

C.3.5 Settings 2–4: Real Datasets with Fitted Covariance Prediction

The synthetic setting validates the theory in the exact model for which it was derived. We now ask a stronger question: does the Gaussian-derived theoretical prediction remain accurate when applied to real, non-Gaussian data? To test this, we use actual images (or VAE latents) as the data distribution xix_{i} and only use the Gaussian approximation for the theoretical variance prediction, not for data generation. We evaluate on CIFAR-10 (pixel space, d=3072d=3072), FFHQ (VAE latents, d=4096d=4096), and CelebA-HQ (VAE latents, d=4096d=4096).

Common procedure.

For each dataset we compute the sample mean μ\mu and sample covariance Σ^=1n−1​∑i(xi−μ)​(xi−μ)⊤\hat{\Sigma}=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i}(x_{i}-\mu)(x_{i}-\mu)^{\top} over the full set of nn available samples (CIFAR-10 in pixel space, CelebA-HQ and FFHQ in VAE-latent space), and form the eigendecomposition Σ^=V​diag​(λ^1,…,λ^d)​V⊤\hat{\Sigma}=V\,\mathrm{diag}(\hat{\lambda}_{1},\dots,\hat{\lambda}_{d})\,V^{\top} with eigenvalues sorted in decreasing order. Given a signal rank kk, we approximate the data covariance with a spiked model by setting the signal subspace Ux=V:,1:kU_{x}=V_{:,1:k}, the spike eigenvalues Λ=diag⁡(λ^1−σ2,…,λ^k−σ2)\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\hat{\lambda}_{1}-\sigma^{2},\dots,\hat{\lambda}_{k}-\sigma^{2}) (clipped to be non-negative), and the isotropic noise variance σ2=1d−k​∑j=k+1dλ^j\sigma^{2}=\frac{1}{d-k}\sum_{j=k+1}^{d}\hat{\lambda}_{j}. These parameters are used solely for the theoretical variance prediction; the data itself is not assumed to be Gaussian. We then sample N=20,000N=20{,}000 triples (εi,xi,ti)(\varepsilon_{i},x_{i},t_{i}) with εi∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)\varepsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), xix_{i} drawn with replacement from the dataset (and centered by subtracting μ\mu), and ti∼Uniform⁡[0,1]t_{i}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[0,1], form the interpolant zi=(1−ti)​εi+ti​xicenteredz_{i}=(1-t_{i})\,\varepsilon_{i}+t_{i}\,x_{i}^{\mathrm{centered}}, and apply the noise-subspace estimator using the PCA-derived U⟂U_{\perp}.

The representative signal rank kk for the per-dataset error distribution plots (Figure 5) is chosen at the 95%95\% cumulative-explained-variance threshold, which falls in the regime where the spectrum transitions from rapid to gradual decay (Figure 3). The scaling sweep additionally varies k∈{10,50,100,200,500,1000,2000}k\in\{10,50,100,200,500,1000,2000\} within each dataset to trace the full range of noise-subspace dimensions, with σ2\sigma^{2} recomputed from the residual spectrum at each kk.

CIFAR-10.

We load all 50,00050{,}000 training images and flatten each 32×32×332\times 32\times 3 image to a d=3,072d=3{,}072-dimensional vector (pixel values in [0,1][0,1]). The 95%95\% explained-variance threshold corresponds to k=217k=217, which is the rank used for the error-distribution panel; the mean absolute error is 0.00620.0062.

FFHQ.

We use VAE latents at d=4,096d=4{,}096 (Stable Diffusion VAE, 4×32×324\times 32\times 32); see Table C.1 for the encoding setup. The 95%95\% explained-variance threshold corresponds to k=2,581k=2{,}581; the mean absolute error is 0.02130.0213.

CelebA-HQ.

We use VAE latents at d=4,096d=4{,}096 from the same Stable Diffusion VAE used for FFHQ; see Table C.1. The 95%95\% explained-variance threshold corresponds to k=2,273k=2{,}273; the mean absolute error is 0.01750.0175.

Results (Figure 5).

Figure 5 shows the error distribution at the 95% explained-variance rank for all four settings. Despite using real, non-Gaussian data, the empirical distributions closely match the Gaussian-derived theoretical prediction in every case, confirming that the bound is tight beyond the Gaussian model. The scaling sweep (not shown in the main figure) further confirms the 1/d−k1/\sqrt{d-k} rate across all datasets. Notably, the VAE latent distributions (FFHQ, CelebA-HQ) have much flatter spectra than CIFAR-10 pixels: 95% explained variance requires k≈2,581k\approx 2{,}581 and k≈2,273k\approx 2{,}273 respectively, compared to k=217k=217 for CIFAR-10 (Figure 3). This means the VAE spreads variance across more components, leaving a smaller effective noise subspace. Despite this, the estimator remains accurate in all cases, likely because the projection onto a high-dimensional noise subspace has a CLT-like averaging effect regardless of the marginal distribution of xix_{i}.

C.4 Time-Localized Estimation Error and the Variance-Clock Critical Point

Theorem 2 requires staying away from the critical point t∗=1/(1+σ2)t^{*}=1/(1+\sigma^{2}) at which the scalar residual-variance clock σ⟂2​(t)=(1−t)2+t2​σ2\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t)=(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}\sigma^{2} has zero derivative. This subsection probes how this caveat manifests on real datasets by (a) locating t∗t^{*} from the fitted residual variance per dataset, and (b) sweeping the noise-subspace estimator across t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] and reporting binned mean absolute error.

Setup.

For each of CIFAR-10, CelebA-HQ, and FFHQ we run PCA on the data, pick kk at the 95%95\% cumulative-explained-variance threshold, and fit σ^⟂,data2=mean⁡(λ^j>k)\hat{\sigma}_{\perp,\mathrm{data}}^{2}=\mathrm{mean}(\hat{\lambda}_{j>k}) from the trailing eigenvalues, giving the predicted clock and its critical point. We then sample t∼Uniform⁡[0,1]t\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[0,1] (with extra mass at t=1t=1 to populate the right edge), draw a real datapoint xx and noise ε∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), form the interpolant z=(1−t)​ε+t​xz=(1-t)\varepsilon+tx, and run the noise-subspace estimator t^​(z)\hat{t}(z) from (6) via the closed-form descending-branch inverter of Appendix B.3 (the minus-sign root of the quadratic). On CelebA-HQ and FFHQ this includes t>t∗t>t^{*}, where the always-descending-branch convention returns the wrong root by construction; the consequences are quantified in the second result below. We use 10510^{5} samples per dataset and report the binned conditional mean absolute error 𝔼⁡[|t^−t|∣t]\mathbb{E}[|\hat{t}-t|\mid t].

Results.

The experiment makes two predictions, one about the geometry of the variance clock and one about the empirical failure mode of the estimator.

The clock’s critical point is dataset-determined and pushed to the data endpoint by small residual variance. Hypothesis: since t∗=1/(1+σ^⟂,data2)t^{*}=1/(1+\hat{\sigma}_{\perp,\mathrm{data}}^{2}) is a monotone function of the fitted residual variance, datasets with small σ^⟂,data2\hat{\sigma}_{\perp,\mathrm{data}}^{2} should place t∗t^{*} near the data endpoint t=1t=1, while datasets with flatter residual spectra (larger σ^⟂,data2\hat{\sigma}_{\perp,\mathrm{data}}^{2}) should move t∗t^{*} into the interior. Validation: the fitted critical points (Table C.3, Figure C.1) span CIFAR-10 t∗≈0.994t^{*}\approx 0.994 down to FFHQ t∗≈0.894t^{*}\approx 0.894: the pixel-space CIFAR-10 has small residual variance and t∗t^{*} at the boundary, while the VAE-latent datasets have flatter residual spectra and t∗t^{*} in the interior.

For t>t∗t>t^{*} the descending-branch inverter returns the reflection 2​t∗−t2t^{*}-t, producing a quantitatively predictable rise in error. Hypothesis: the variance clock σ⟂2​(t)=(1+σ2)​(t−t∗)2+σ⟂2​(t∗)\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t)=(1+\sigma^{2})(t-t^{*})^{2}+\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t^{*}) is a parabola symmetric around t∗t^{*}, so for any σ^⟂2≥σ⟂2​(t∗)\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}\geq\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t^{*}) the two preimages are t±=t∗±δt_{\pm}=t^{*}\pm\delta with δ=(σ^⟂2−σ⟂2​(t∗))/(1+σ2)\delta=\sqrt{(\hat{\sigma}_{\perp}^{2}-\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t^{*}))/(1+\sigma^{2})}. The minus-root inverter returns t−t_{-}, so when the true t>t∗t>t^{*} the estimator returns the reflection 2​t∗−t2t^{*}-t rather than tt, giving error

|t^−t|≈ 2​(t−t∗)for ​t>t∗.|\hat{t}-t|\;\approx\;2(t-t^{*})\quad\text{for }t>t^{*}.

We therefore predict three things on the binned-MAE plot: (i) error stays small for t<t∗t<t^{*}, (ii) error rises with slope 22 starting near t=t∗t=t^{*}, and (iii) the right-edge peak equals 2​(1−t∗)2(1-t^{*}) — predicted to be ≈0.012\approx 0.012 for CIFAR-10, ≈0.194\approx 0.194 for CelebA-HQ, and ≈0.212\approx 0.212 for FFHQ. Validation: on CelebA-HQ and FFHQ (Figure C.2) the rising-error region begins near the dataset-specific t∗t^{*} rather than at the right endpoint, with peak magnitudes matching the dataset-dependent 2​(1−t∗)2(1-t^{*}) prediction. CIFAR-10’s predicted peak (0.0120.012) is small enough that the branch-mismatch effect is subdominant; any observed residual rise on CIFAR-10 instead reflects model-misspecification: as t→1t\to 1 the marginal of ztz_{t} approaches the data marginal, which is non-Gaussian and not perfectly described by the spiked-covariance fit used to compute σ⟂2​(t)\sigma_{\perp}^{2}(t).

C.5 Closed-Form Variance Decomposition on the Spiked Gaussian

This experiment underlies Figure 6. It validates Theorem 3 (equivalently, Theorem B.5) in a setting where the ambient and signal dimensions can be controlled directly, so the predicted separation of scales between the coupling variance (Term II) and the time-blindness gap (Term III) is observable without confounds from model capacity or data distribution.

Setup.

We use the spiked Gaussian model throughout: ε∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), x∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ)x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma) with Σ=diag⁡(λ,…,λ,σ2,…,σ2)\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda,\dots,\lambda,\sigma^{2},\dots,\sigma^{2}) (the first kk coordinates are signal with variance λ\lambda, the remaining d−kd-k are isotropic noise with variance σ2\sigma^{2}), z=(1−t)​ε+t​xz=(1-t)\varepsilon+tx, and u=x−εu=x-\varepsilon. Default parameters are λ=10\lambda=10, σ2=0.01\sigma^{2}=0.01, with t∼Uniform⁡[τ,1−τ]t\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[\tau,1-\tau], τ=0.15\tau=0.15. Because Σ\Sigma is diagonal and ε,x\varepsilon,x are independent, the pairs (zi,ui)(z_{i},u_{i}) are jointly Gaussian and independent across coordinates, so all quantities of interest reduce to sums of per-coordinate integrals and admit either closed forms or low-variance numerical estimators.

Term I: learnable error.

The learnable error is the variance of u=x−εu=x-\varepsilon with no conditioning, which has the closed form

tr⁡(Cov⁡(u))=tr⁡(Σ+Id)=k⁡(λ+1)+(d−k)​(σ2+1).\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{Cov}(u))\;=\;\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma+I_{d})\;=\;k(\lambda+1)+(d-k)(\sigma^{2}+1).

This is the only one of the three terms that admits a fully closed-form integral, since it does not depend on tt.

Term II: coupling variance 𝒞π\mathcal{C}_{\pi}.

Per coordinate, joint Gaussianity of (zi,ui)(z_{i},u_{i}) gives the standard regression-variance closed form

Var⁡(ui∣zi,t)=(Si+1)−(t​Si−(1−t))2vi​(t),vi​(t):=(1−t)2+t2​Si,\mathrm{Var}(u_{i}\mid z_{i},t)\;=\;(S_{i}+1)-\frac{(tS_{i}-(1-t))^{2}}{v_{i}(t)},\qquad v_{i}(t)\;:=\;(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}S_{i},

with Si∈{λ,σ2}S_{i}\in\{\lambda,\sigma^{2}\} depending on whether ii is a signal or noise coordinate. This expression does not depend on ziz_{i} (Gaussian–Gaussian conditioning), so summing over coordinates produces a deterministic function of tt. We integrate it against t∼Unif⁡[τ,1−τ]t\sim\mathrm{Unif}[\tau,1-\tau] by the trapezoidal rule on a 20002000-point grid to obtain 𝒞π\mathcal{C}_{\pi}.

Total time-blind variance 𝔼z​[tr⁡(Var⁡(u∣z))]\mathbb{E}_{z}[\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{Var}(u\mid z))].

This is the irreducible error when tt is not observed. Unlike 𝒞π\mathcal{C}_{\pi} it does not reduce to a closed-form integral, because Var⁡(u∣z)\mathrm{Var}(u\mid z) depends on the full posterior p⁡(t∣z)p(t\mid z). We estimate it with a hybrid Monte-Carlo / grid scheme.

We draw N=2×105N=2\times 10^{5} outer samples (t,ε,x)(t,\varepsilon,x) with t∼Unif⁡[τ,1−τ]t\sim\mathrm{Unif}[\tau,1-\tau], ε∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), and x∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ)x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma), and form z=(1−t)​ε+t​xz=(1-t)\varepsilon+tx. For each such zz, we evaluate the posterior on a 20002000-point grid {t′}\{t^{\prime}\} in [τ,1−τ][\tau,1-\tau] via

p⁡(t′∣z)∝∏i𝒩⁡(zi, 0,vi​(t′)).p(t^{\prime}\mid z)\;\propto\;\prod_{i}\mathcal{N}\!\bigl(z_{i};\,0,\,v_{i}(t^{\prime})\bigr).

From this posterior, we compute the conditional mean of each coordinate of uu as

𝔼⁡[ui∣z]=zi​∑t′αi​(t′)​p​(t′∣z),αi​(t′):=t′​Si−(1−t′)vi​(t′),\mathbb{E}[u_{i}\mid z]\;=\;z_{i}\sum_{t^{\prime}}\alpha_{i}(t^{\prime})\,p(t^{\prime}\mid z),\qquad\alpha_{i}(t^{\prime})\;:=\;\frac{t^{\prime}S_{i}-(1-t^{\prime})}{v_{i}(t^{\prime})},

and the conditional second moment as

𝔼⁡[ui2∣z]=∑t′[Var⁡(ui∣z,t′)+(αi​(t′)​zi)2]​p​(t′∣z).\mathbb{E}[u_{i}^{2}\mid z]\;=\;\sum_{t^{\prime}}\bigl[\mathrm{Var}(u_{i}\mid z,t^{\prime})+(\alpha_{i}(t^{\prime})\,z_{i})^{2}\bigr]\,p(t^{\prime}\mid z).

The per-coordinate conditional variance follows by subtraction:

Var⁡(ui∣z)=𝔼⁡[ui2∣z]−(𝔼⁡[ui∣z])2.\mathrm{Var}(u_{i}\mid z)\;=\;\mathbb{E}[u_{i}^{2}\mid z]-\bigl(\mathbb{E}[u_{i}\mid z]\bigr)^{2}.

Summing across coordinates and averaging across the NN samples of zz gives the estimator of 𝔼z​[tr⁡(Var⁡(u∣z))]\mathbb{E}_{z}[\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{Var}(u\mid z))]. All arithmetic is performed in double precision to avoid numerical cancellation when Term III is orders of magnitude smaller than Term II.

Term III: time-blindness gap Δ\Delta.

The time-blindness gap is recovered by the law of total variance as the residual between the total time-blind variance and the coupling variance: Δ=𝔼z​[tr⁡(Var⁡(u∣z))]−𝒞π\Delta=\mathbb{E}_{z}[\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{Var}(u\mid z))]-\mathcal{C}_{\pi}. This decomposition lets us extract Δ\Delta without needing a separate Monte-Carlo estimator for it.

Sweep.

We sweep both axes of the (d,k)(d,k) grid simultaneously: k∈{1,2,4,…,1024}k\in\{1,2,4,\dots,1024\} and d∈{2,4,8,…,1024}d\in\{2,4,8,\dots,1024\} (log-spaced powers of two), restricted to k<dk<d since the construction requires a non-empty noise subspace. At each (d,k)(d,k) we recompute all three terms from scratch. From this (d,k)(d,k) table we extract three slices for Figure 6: the column at fixed d=1024d=1024 sweeping kk (left panel), the entire grid as a heatmap of Term III (center panel), and the row at fixed k=64k=64 sweeping dd (right panel).

Results (Figure 6).

The right panel reproduces the asymptotic gap-collapse: at k=64k=64 fixed, Term III decays from ∼2\sim\!2 at the smallest admissible dd to below ∼0.5\sim\!0.5 by d=1024d=1024, while Terms I and II stay bounded over the same sweep. The left panel shows the complementary regime: at d=1024d=1024 fixed, all three terms grow with kk, but Term III grows fastest because the noise subspace d−kd-k is shrinking, sharpening the prediction that the variance-based identifiability mechanism degrades as k→dk\to d. The center heatmap shows both regimes simultaneously: Δ\Delta is small along the upper-right edge (k≪dk\ll d) and large along the diagonal (k≈dk\approx d), tracing the same geometry across the (d,k)(d,k) plane. Together, these slices give a quantitative signature of Theorem 3.
